item.title: Journalist found dead at Samakal Barisal bureau office
item.description:
Police recovered the hanging body of senior journalist and former Daily Samakal Barisal bureau chief Pulak Chatterjee, 57, from the newspaper’s Barisal bureau office on Friday evening.
The body was recovered from the office on Parara Road in the city.
According to local sources, Pulak Chatterjee had been dismissed from Samakal about three years ago. He was a former general secretary of the Barisal Press Club and had previously worked for Daily Jugantor for many years. He is survived by his wife and a daughter.
Suman Chowdhury, chief staff reporter at Samakal’s Barisal office, said Pulak had a key to the office and often visited it during the day or at night.
“His wife called me in the afternoon and said he was not answering his phone. When I came to the office in the evening, I found the door locked from inside. Looking through a gap, I saw him hanging with a noose around his neck. I immediately informed the police,” he said.
Police later broke open the door and recovered the body.
Pulak had most recently served as Samakal’s Barisal bureau chief. He had reportedly been mentally distressed since losing his job at the newspaper about three years ago.
Al Mamun-ul Islam, officer-in-charge of Barisal Kotwali Model Police Station, said police initially suspected suicide.
“The exact cause of death will be known after the autopsy report,” he said.

item.title: Egg, vegetable prices rise by Tk10-40
item.description:
Prices of eggs and several vegetables have increased in Dhaka markets over the past week, while fish and meat prices have remained largely stable.
A dozen eggs, which sold for Tk145-150 last week, are now priced at Tk155-160, marking a Tk10 increase. Retailers are selling individual eggs for around Tk13-14.
Among vegetables, green chilli and yardlong bean prices have risen by Tk40 per kg each to Tk160 and Tk120, respectively. Round eggplant has increased by Tk20 to Tk140 per kg, while cucumber has risen by Tk20-30 to Tk80.
However, tomato and papaya prices have fallen. Tomatoes now sell for Tk100 per kg, down from Tk120-140, while papaya has dropped from Tk40 to Tk30.
Prices of ridge gourd, bitter gourd, sponge gourd, snake gourd and pointed gourd have remained largely unchanged at around Tk80 per kg.
The situation was observed during visits to several markets in the capital on Friday.
Meanwhile, fish prices showed no major changes. Sellers said prices of some varieties fluctuate by Tk20-30 per kg from one day to another.
Pangash is selling for Tk230 per kg, telapia Tk260, shrimp Tk800-900, pabda Tk350-450, large rui Tk450-500 and tengra Tk700.
Vetki is priced at Tk400-550 per kg, mrigel Tk250-300, baim Tk600-800, local koi Tk700-800, farmed koi Tk300 and poa Tk260. Farmed shing is selling for Tk300-450 per kg depending on size, while medium-sized rui costs Tk270-350.
When asked about fish prices, Sheikh Rafiqul said, “I bought fish for the month. Prices seem Tk20-30 higher per kilogram. The fish market is never stable, with prices fluctuating almost every day.”
The price hike has put the greatest strain on low-income and limited-income households. Abul Hossain, a day labourer, said, “We used to buy pangas and telapia, but even those have become expensive. Prices are rising day by day, with no sign of coming down.”
Meanwhile, beef is being sold at Tk800 per kilogram, almost unchanged from the previous week. Broiler chicken is also being sold at Tk180-190 per kilogram, the same as last week. However, prices of Sonali, hybrid and layer chickens have fallen by around Tk10 per kilogram.
Rocky Ahmed, a chicken seller at Rayerbazar, said, “Chicken prices were slightly lower this week than last week. Still, we are selling them at Tk180-190 per kilogram.”
Egg trader Masum said, “Egg prices have not fallen; rather, they have increased. A dozen eggs are now selling for Tk155-160.”
Zahidur Rahman, a private-sector employee who came to Raysahib Bazar to shop on his weekly day off, said, “I found vegetable prices considerably higher than last week. Many vegetables that were available at lower prices last week are now more expensive. This is naturally increasing our household expenses.”
Rafiqullah Khan, a vegetable seller at Narinda Bazar, attributed the price rise to reduced supply following several days of rain.
“Several days of rain have reduced the supply of vegetables from farms and markets. Lower supply has pushed up wholesale prices, which has affected retail prices as well,” he said.
“Eggplant is currently selling at Tk140 per kilogram, the highest price in today’s market, while papaya is available at Tk30 per kilogram. If the weather improves, supply will increase and vegetable prices may come down,” he added.

item.title: BGB foils BSF bid to push 12 into Bangladesh through Satkhira
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) on Friday successfully foiled an attempt by India's Border Security Force (BSF) to illegally push 10 to 12 unidentified individuals into Bangladesh through the Kalindi River border in Satkhira district amid adverse weather and heavy rain.
Members of Char Sahebkhali BSF Camp under the 77 BSF Battalion attempted the illegal push-in using one country boat and one speed boat on Friday morning at a place named 'Chhot Banshjharia Mini Forest' in a mid-river char area of the Kalindi River, located approximately 3.5 kilometers south of Khurmi Border Outpost (BOP) under the Nildumur Battalion (17 BGB), according to a BGB press release.
Upon spotting the activity, a patrol team from Khurmi BOP immediately dispatched a speed boat to the scene despite heavy rainfall and blocked their entry into Bangladeshi territory. Faced with BGB's firm stance, BSF members failed in their attempt and eventually took the 10 to 12 individuals back into Indian territory at around 11 a.m.
Lieutenant Colonel Khandakar Abu Sahal Abdullah, commanding officer of Nildumur Battalion (17 BGB), said that 17 BGB is maintaining maximum alertness, professionalism and responsibility to ensure national border security.
"No individual or group will be allowed to illegally enter Bangladeshi territory," Abdullah said, emphasizing that any push-in attempt violating international border management guidelines, existing laws and bilateral agreements will be strictly resisted.

item.title: Gaza documentary gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice Film Festival
item.description:
If last year's Venice Film Festival spotlighted "The Voice of Hind Rajab," this year's edition has turned its attention to "NAZA," a documentary exploring the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
Directed by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the film received an overwhelmingly positive response following its premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday.
According to AFP, "NAZA" received a 25-minute standing ovation after the screening, reportedly setting a new record at the festival. The audience continued applauding the directing duo, surpassing the 23-minute ovation given to "The Voice of Hind Rajab" last year. The docu-drama tells the story of the killing of a five-year-old Palestinian girl by Israeli forces.
Earlier, as Abraham and Szor walked the red carpet toward the screening venue, spectators could be heard chanting both "Free Palestine!" and "Free Israel!" The strong response has positioned "NAZA" as a frontrunner for Venice's top prize.
"The Voice of Hind Rajab" was similarly considered a favorite for the festival's top award last year after receiving an enthusiastic response. However, it ultimately won the festival's second prize, amid reports of divisions among the jury.
For years, the length of a standing ovation has been regarded as an indicator of a film's reception at major international film festivals. AFP noted that while such ovations can be manipulated, they can still offer insight into the impact a film has on festival audiences and critics.
"NAZA" features testimonies from 24 Israeli military insiders, including intelligence officers and soldiers, who describe their experiences during the war in Gaza and what they allege was the systematic killing of Palestinian civilians.
The film was shot secretly over three years on rooftops across Tel Aviv. The identities of those interviewed have been concealed through digital alterations to their voices and appearances.
Speaking at a press conference in Venice on Thursday, Abraham said the filmmakers primarily asked the Israeli officers and soldiers to describe in detail what they had done.
He said: "Of course, there were other questions that arose, but the principal question was a question of detail — sketch it for us, we want to know how it worked. And sometimes just asking the question, you get answers."
The film's title refers to an Israeli military acronym used as shorthand for civilian casualties, including men, women and children.
"NAZA" builds on investigations published between 2023 and 2025 by Israeli-Palestinian magazine 972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.
At the Venice press conference, Szor also addressed the filmmakers' decision to make a documentary based on information that had already been reported and published.

item.title: Solar power lights up lives on Rampal char amid electricity crisis
item.description:
Just across the river from one of the country’s largest thermal power plants, hundreds of families on a remote char in Rampal upazila of Bagerhat are turning to solar energy to keep their homes lit amid an electricity crisis.
At Kaigardashkathi Char, around 800 fishing families live with unreliable power supply and dwindling fish stocks. Many households now rely on solar panels despite living close to the 1,320MW Maitree Super Thermal Power Plant, which supplies electricity to the national grid.
“Look across the river. You can see the thermal power plant. It supplies electricity to the whole country, but we are on this side. Why don’t we get electricity?” fisherman Al Amin Fakir said. “We have to depend on solar panels. At the same time, we can no longer find enough fish in the river to support our families,” he added.
Residents allege that hot-water discharge from the power plant has contributed to declining fish availability, threatening their traditional livelihoods.
Tania Begum, a housewife, said she used to catch enough fish from the river to support her family while her husband went to sea. “Before the power plant was built, I could catch enough fish here. Now I can spend the whole day casting a net and catch almost nothing,” she said.
Rabeya Begum, who lives behind the power plant, said she could not afford an electricity connection. “Last year, an NGO gave me a 50-watt solar panel. That is what I use for lighting at night,” she said.
Abdul Ahad, a line worker with Bagerhat Palli Bidyut Samity, said residential consumers had to pay a security deposit of Tk465 per kilowatt. Including line and meter charges, a household could spend Tk3,000-Tk3,500 to obtain a connection.
Gourambha Union Parishad administrator Md Habibur Rahman said prolonged waterlogging in settlements behind the plant made electricity connections difficult. “People are using solar panels with support from NGOs and through their own initiatives. Amid the electricity crisis, more people are now considering solar power,” he said.
Solar energy is also creating new income opportunities for women in Bagerhat.
Marina Juthi, executive director of IRV, said eight solar-powered incubators had been provided in Bagerhat Sadar and Rampal. The machines allow women to hatch chicken eggs, produce chicks and sell them from home.
Seven solar-powered water pumps have also been provided to women’s groups for dry-season irrigation, helping sustain agriculture and increase household incomes.
Marina said women should be treated not merely as beneficiaries but as leaders of renewable-energy initiatives, calling for government incentives and greater support.
However, Bangladesh-India Friendship Power Company Director Anwarul Azim rejected allegations that the plant releases hot water into the river. “No hot water from the plant is discharged into the river. It is stored in a reservoir and reused after cooling,” he said.
For residents of Kaigardashkathi, solar power is no longer simply an alternative. It has become an essential source of light—and an increasingly important tool for sustaining livelihoods in a community still struggling for reliable access to electricity.

item.title: Kabir-Lalon festival begins Dhaka leg of eight-division tour
item.description:
A month-long festival celebrating the philosophy, spiritual traditions and music of Sant Kabir and Lalon Fakir began in the capital on Friday, with programs scheduled across all eight divisions until October 30.
Organized by Lalon Bishwosangha with the support of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, the Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Festival opened at the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy field in Dhaka on Friday.
Kishoreganj-4 lawmaker Fazlur Rahman inaugurated the festival. State Minister for Cultural Affairs **Ali Newaz Mahmood Khyom** attended the event as the chief guest, while Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi was present as the special guest. Professor Anisuzzaman, chairman of Lalon Bishwosangha, chaired the opening program.
The opening program featured discussions on different aspects of Kabir and Lalon’s philosophy, spiritual traditions and music, along with performances of bhabsangeet, or devotional folk music.
Artists from different traditions, including Kabirpanthi, Ravidaspanthi and Nanakpanthi performers, took part in the festival. Artists from the University of Dhaka’s Department of Music and the Kabir-Lalon Musical Mission also performed.
Following the Dhaka opening, the festival will travel to different parts of the country. The Barisal program will be held at the district Shilpakala Academy auditorium on September 18, followed by the Khulna program on September 19.
The Mymensingh division program will be held at the Sherpur District Shilpakala Academy auditorium on September 25. The festival will then move to Rajshahi on October 2 and Rangpur on October 4.
A program will be held at the Chittagong District Shilpakala Academy auditorium on October 23. The festival will conclude in Sreemangal, representing the Sylhet division, on October 30 at the Sreemangal District Council Multipurpose Auditorium.
The organizers said the festival aims to bring the philosophy and musical traditions of Kabir and Lalon to people across the country through music, discussions and performances representing various spiritual traditions.

item.title: Nahid: Gas, power crises, corruption persist since Hasina era

National Citizen Party (NCP) Convener and Opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam has said gas and electricity shortages, along with corruption, have persisted since Sheikh Hasina’s tenure.
“These problems still exist, and the opposition will remain on the streets until the country’s gas, power and law-and-order situation returns to normal,” he said.
Nahid made the remarks at view- exchange meeting with locals at Satarkul School and College in his Dhaka-11 constituency on Friday afternoon. Earlier, he visited several neighbourhoods in the area.
He said the ongoing crises could have been addressed more effectively if the government had taken appropriate initiatives over the past seven months.
Referring to the last election, Nahid said voters in Satarkul had rejected extortionists and would not elect them in the future either.
He also alleged that opposition lawmakers do not receive development allocations on par with those from the ruling party, making it difficult to plan development projects for their constituencies.
“Development allocations should be distributed equally between the government and opposition parties,” he said.

item.title: Woman’s body found in suitcase under Gazipur culvert
item.description:
The decomposed lower half of the body was found inside a suitcase floating in the water beneath the culvert along the Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway in Sadar upazila.
Police later recovered the woman’s head and other body parts from a jute sack floating nearby. Locals first spotted the suitcase and alerted police after noticing a human leg protruding from it.
Police then recovered the lower half of the body from inside the suitcase.
Later, they found a jute sack floating in the water near the culvert. A search of the sack revealed the woman’s head and other body parts.
Police suspect the woman was murdered elsewhere and that the perpetrators dismembered her body before putting the remains in the suitcase and sack and dumping them beneath the culvert at night.
Joydebpur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Al Mamun confirmed the matter.
He said the victim’s identity and the motive for the killing could not immediately be established. The remains were sent to the morgue of Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Medical College Hospital in Gazipur for autopsy.
“The investigation will determine where and why the woman was killed,” the OC said, adding that efforts were underway to identify the victim and arrest those involved.

item.title: Sifat murder case: Three more accused confess
item.description:
Three more accused in the murder case of Qatar expatriate Sifat Ullah, who was allegedly called to a house in the capital’s Madartek area and killed, have given confessional statements before a court.
Sajidul Islam Sajid was sent to jail after completing his remand.
On Friday, case investigation officer SI Golap Uddin Mahmud of Sabujbagh Police Station produced four accused, including Sajid, before the court.
Al Amin Hossain Joy, Tuhin and Yasin Hossain Sifat agreed to give confessional statements, while the IO sought to have their statements recorded and Sajid sent to jail.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Siddiq Azad recorded the statements of the three accused. The three were subsequently sent to jail along with Sajid, said SI Mominul Islam of the prosecution department.
On Monday, the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) arrested Joy from Jhilpara in Shahjahanpur and Sajid from Kayetpara Balur Math. The following day, a court granted three-day remand for Sajid and Joy.
On the same day, Nafiza Sheikh Neha gave a confessional statement before the court.
Tuhin and Sifat were arrested on Thursday.
On September 6, expatriate Sifat was allegedly called out of his home and hacked to death by a group of assailants on a road near the Baraitala culvert in Madartek Adarshpara under Sabujbagh Police Station.
Sifat’s father, Zainal Abedin, filed a case with Sabujbagh Police Station last Monday, accusing seven people. Apart from Neha, Sajid and Joy, the other accused are Arafat, Tuhin, Anik and Rabbi.
According to the case statement, Sifat was in a relationship with Neha. He had returned to Bangladesh from Qatar about one and a half months earlier.
Later, Sifat learned that Neha was also in a relationship with Sajid, leading to a dispute between Sifat and Neha.
On September 6, Neha allegedly called Sajid over the issue. At around 3:15pm that day, Sifat went by motorcycle to the Baraitala culvert area in Madartek Adarshpara, where the accused allegedly attacked him.
They reportedly hacked him indiscriminately and left him injured on the road.
Locals rescued Sifat and took him to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
Sifat hailed from the Dholairpar area of Jatrabari. His father is Zainal Abedin.

item.title: Three held with gold jewellery worth Tk 1.37 crore at Dhaka airport
item.description:
Airport Armed Police Battalion (APBn) detained three people with 861.8 grams of gold jewellery, equivalent to around 74 bhoris, at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
The detainees were identified as Md Nasir Molla, 40, Sohag Sheikh, 24, and Md Hasan Mia, 23.
According to APBn, the three were seen moving suspiciously on the footpath on the northern side of the airport roundabout late Thursday night.
Sensing the presence of police, they allegedly tried to flee discreetly, but APBn personnel detained them.
A body search led to the recovery of 861.8 grams of gold jewellery in their possession. The jewellery was made of 21- and 22-carat gold and had an estimated market value of Tk 1,36,86,160.
During preliminary interrogation, the detainees reportedly said the jewellery had been brought into Bangladesh from different countries through unidentified passengers for the purpose of smuggling.
APBn said the three had allegedly been involved in gold smuggling at the airport for a long time.
A regular case was filed against them with the Airport Police Station on Thursday.
The case alleges that the three, in collusion with one another and with the assistance of unidentified passengers, brought the gold into the country illegally for smuggling while evading government revenue and kept it in their possession.
Mohammad Rezaul Kabir, superintendent of police of Airport (13) APBn, said the force remains committed to maintaining security at the airport and preventing crime.
“We remain active and vigilant in preventing smuggling and controlling other crimes. Airport APBn is determined to prevent gold and drug smuggling, and our operations to stop any form of smuggling through the airport will continue,” he said.

item.title: Egg nutrition depends on feed, not shell colour
item.description:
Shoppers picking between brown and white eggs at supermarkets often assume shell colour signals nutritional value, but experts say the belief has no scientific basis.
According to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), shell colour depends on the breed of hen, not on the egg's nutritional content. Leghorn, White Rock and Cornish hens lay white eggs, while Rhode Island Red, New Hampshire and Plymouth Rock hens lay brown eggs. Araucana hens, native to South America, lay eggs that are blue or green.
The colour difference comes down to pigmentation. Brown eggshells get their colour from protoporphyrin IX, a compound derived from blood haem, while blue eggs carry a different pigment called biliverdin. A 2015 review found that pigment levels in brown eggs can also vary with a hen's age, strain, housing conditions, certain diseases, and stress.
The USDA states that nutrient levels are not significantly different between white and brown shell eggs. Claims that blue or green eggs from Araucana hens contain less cholesterol than other eggs have also not been proven by research.
Egg size, however, does affect nutritional content regardless of colour. The USDA's Certified Egg Facts note that jumbo eggs contain approximately 90 calories and 8 grams of protein, compared to 60 calories and 6 grams of protein in medium eggs.
Shell colour also has little bearing on taste. Freshness, the hen's diet, and cooking method have a far greater effect on flavour than the colour of the shell.
What does affect nutritional value is how the hen is raised. Hens with access to sunlight and open-air movement may produce eggs with higher vitamin D content than those raised in cages.
Enriching a hen's feed with omega-3-rich ingredients such as flaxseed can increase the omega-3 fatty acid content of its eggs, and adding vitamin-rich feed can raise specific vitamin levels as well.
Brown eggs have historically carried a higher price, partly because brown-egg-laying breeds were traditionally larger birds that consumed more feed and, in some cases, produced fewer eggs, raising production costs.
Although production methods have since changed, the perception that brown eggs are more nutritious — along with the fact that many organic and free-range eggs happen to be brown — continues to keep their market price higher.
Nutritionists recommend that shoppers focus less on shell colour and more on freshness, storage conditions, and what the hen was fed when choosing eggs.
There is no scientific basis for the belief that brown eggs are more nutritious than white ones.v

item.title: Apurba, Niha pair reunite on screen after break
item.description:
Ziaul Faruq Apurba and Naznin Niha, who have appeared together in several popular television dramas, are set to reunite on screen after a break of several months.
The pair first worked together in Zakaria Soukhin's "Mon Duari" in early 2025. The drama has since garnered more than 40 million views. They later appeared together in productions including "Meghbalika," "Ghran" and "Ochena Ami," each of which has reportedly crossed 10 million views.
There had been no news of the two shooting together since March. Following Eid-ul-Fitr, Apurba spent an extended period in the United States with his family, while Niha also took time away to focus on her family. During this period, Niha announced her engagement in a Facebook post and may marry later this year.
The pair are now returning with a new drama written and directed by S R Mozumder. The project is yet to be titled, with shooting having begun in late August. The production is expected to require around 12 days of filming.
According to the director, portions of the drama have already been shot in Cox's Bazar, with filming set to continue in Dhaka.
Speaking to Prothom Alo, Mozumder said: "This is my 24th project with Apurba bhai, but my first time working with Apurba and Niha as a pair. I have always received tremendous support from Apurba bhai. He is not only a brilliant actor but also a wonderful person. He remains involved in different aspects of the work and is always supportive."
This also marks Mozumder's first collaboration with Niha.
"She has a strong desire to do good work. I think audiences will see something new from this pair," he said. "We spent considerable time on pre-production and are now shooting. We will also take our time with post-production. I believe audiences will enjoy it."
The director said the drama explores time and relationships, beginning with misunderstandings and resentment within a family before developing into a mystery years later.
"Some mistakes in life leave no way of going back. We are trying to tell a different kind of relationship story through that idea," Mozumder said, adding that Apurba and Niha will portray a married couple.
The nearly two-hour drama also features Abu Hurayra Tanvir in a guest role. It will be released on CD Choice's YouTube channel, although a release date has yet to be announced.
Apurba and Niha are also expected to appear together in two more upcoming dramas.

item.title: BTS wraps record-breaking North America tour
item.description:
South Korean group BTS concluded the North America leg of its “Arirang” world tour with four shows at SoFi Stadium on September 1, 2, 5 and 6, drawing a combined crowd of approximately 282,000.
The North America leg ran across 12 cities, comprising 31 concerts, all of which sold out in advance. Total attendance across the leg reached approximately 1.92 million.
The tour opened in Tampa, Florida, and closed in Los Angeles.
With the SoFi Stadium shows, BTS has now performed 8 concerts at the venue since 2021, including 4 dates from its “Permission to Dance on Stage” tour that year. The group holds the record for the most concerts by any act at SoFi Stadium, with cumulative attendance across those 8 shows reaching approximately 496,000 — also a venue record.
Several city and state governments issued formal recognitions during the tour. Los Angeles declared “BTS Week” from September 1 to 8. Toronto marked “BTS Weekend” on August 22 and 23, temporarily renaming a stretch of Yonge Street “BTS Boulevard.”
Illinois designated August 27 and 28 as “BTS Day in Illinois” to coincide with the group’s Chicago concerts. El Paso, Texas, held “El Paso BTS Weekend” on May 2 and 3, and awarded the group its “Estimado Amigo” honor in recognition of its contribution to the city’s tourism and international profile.
Maryland Governor Wes Moore also welcomed the group in a video message, saying the seven-member act brings people together across culture, geography and language.
In Mexico City, President Claudia Sheinbaum hosted BTS at the National Palace during the group’s concert stop there. Approximately 50,000 fans gathered outside the palace to greet the group.
At the Los Angeles shows, fans marked the birthdays of members Jungkook and RM, born September 1 and September 12 respectively, singing birthday songs during the concerts. The stadium was lit in gold and blue, colors chosen to match Jungkook’s solo album “Golden” and RM’s “Indigo.”
At the final show, member J-Hope said the tour’s opening night in Tampa felt as though it had happened only recently, adding that the group had long anticipated returning to North America and that the time had passed quickly.
BTS will next perform in South America, opening with concerts in Bogota, Colombia, on October 2 and 3. The tour continues to Lima, Santiago, Buenos Aires and Sao Paulo. The stops in Colombia, Peru and Argentina will mark the group’s first full-lineup concerts in those countries

item.title: Children increasingly used as drug carriers
item.description:
Children are increasingly being used to transport and sell drugs, with some allegedly forced to carry yaba inside their bodies, raising concerns among crime experts, sociologists and human rights activists.
In a recent case, two children were allegedly made to swallow yaba capsules and taken from Cox’s Bazar to Chittagong. After the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) arrested them, 6,615 yaba pills were recovered from their stomachs at Chittagong Medical College Hospital. They were later produced before a court and sent to a child correctional facility.
Chittagong Civil Surgeon Mohammad Sajedur Rahman said yaba is wrapped in plastic and packed into small, capsule-like packets before being swallowed.
“Carrying drugs inside a child’s body in this way is extremely risky,” he said.
If a capsule gets stuck in the intestine or bursts, the drug can quickly spread through the body, causing poisoning, serious health complications and even death, he added.
A recent visit to Gulistan, Karwan Bazar, Moghbazar, Geneva Camp in Mohammadpur, Basila and Natun Bazar-Bhatara found street children being used to sell drugs. Meanwhile, five children from four families in a village in Katiadi, Kishoreganj, were allegedly sold to raise money to buy drugs.
According to the Department of Narcotics Control (DNC), children account for around 25% of those involved in drug smuggling, transportation and sales in Bangladesh, most of them under 16. The DNC said traders prefer children because they are cheap to employ and less likely to attract law enforcement attention.
Experts said children involved in the drug trade face serious risks while losing access to education, healthcare and a normal childhood.
Visits to slums, transport terminals, railway-side areas and low-income settlements found many street children involved in criminal activities, including drug transportation and smuggling.
Drugs are openly sold around Karwan Bazar, Moghbazar and Geneva Camp after evening. At Geneva Camp, children take buyers to specific alleys while others carry drugs, earning Tk20 to Tk50 per transaction.
A child living there said he does not attend school or have a job, so he takes drug buyers to different alleys at night.
Many street children were also seen consuming Dandy on the road island between Farmgate and Shahbagh, with some carrying drugs. Several said they collect plastic bottles, including from the Karwan Bazar railway line, during the day and sleep on the streets at night. They use the money to buy food, glue and Dandy.
Residents said most children in Geneva Camp do not attend school because their parents cannot afford it and do not encourage them to study. Taking advantage of their poverty, traders allegedly recruit children through their families. Residents said children are paid less, are less likely to be suspected and face relatively little punishment if caught. They estimated more than 100 children and adolescents from the camp are involved.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune yesterday afternoon, DNC Deputy Director (Operations) Mukul Jyoti Chakma said operations against drug smuggling were continuing.
“Several groups are using street children and children from poor families in drug smuggling. When children are caught, we take a humanitarian approach and ensure appropriate protection for them through the legal process,” he said.
He said the DNC was working with the Department of Social Services on child-related issues.
“Several projects are being implemented by the Department of Social Services. Under these projects, children are being provided education, healthcare, sports and vocational training,” he said.
Regarding the Chittagong incident, RAB-7 Commander Lt Col Md Mostafizur Rahman said each small capsule contained around 40 to 50 yaba pills.
A person paid each child Tk4,000, or Tk8,000 in total, and promised additional money after delivery, he said. The children told RAB they had previously travelled to Chittagong twice carrying yaba in the same way.
“This shows that the syndicate repeatedly used them to transport drugs through this dangerous method. We are working to catch the group,” he added.
Dhaka University teacher and crime expert Dr Touhidul Haque told Dhaka Tribune yesterday afternoon that such incidents were not new.
“Drugs are being concealed inside children’s stomachs, under their skin and through their rectums. Such incidents have happened before,” he said.
He said drug traders exploit disadvantaged, extremely poor and street children.
“These children and their families are taking risks for money, which can even lead to their deaths. Since these children do not have the ability to protest or resist, those involved are taking advantage of that,” he said.
“There is a mindset that these children have no future and that it does not matter whether they live or die,” he said, urging the government to ensure they grow up in a healthy and safe environment and strictly punish groups using them.
Human rights activist Nur Khan Liton told Dhaka Tribune that children are used worldwide to carry drugs and weapons, with law enforcement agencies less likely to suspect them.
“Social resistance must be built to protect children. People must be made aware. The government must also come forward to protect extremely poor children, children separated from their families and street children,” he said.
Supreme Court lawyer Humayun Kabir told Dhaka Tribune that the Children Act 2013 provides a separate justice system for children.
“Especially if it is found that a drug dealer has used a child, the child should not only be seen as a drug carrier but should also be investigated as a trafficking victim,” he said.
He said some parents are involved with drug gangs and could send children to carry drugs again, while others face abuse or extreme neglect. In such cases, courts may consider correctional facilities safer.
However, he said detention alone was insufficient.
“There must be arrangements for their education, healthcare, treatment, vocational training and sports. Most importantly, they need counselling,” he added.

item.title: Trivedi: People-centric issues should not be allowed to get stuck
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi has called for keeping trade, cultural exchanges and people-to-people connectivity between Bangladesh and India moving forward, saying such issues should not be held back by political developments.
Talking to reporters after a cultural programme in Dhaka on Friday evening, he said issues would continue to be discussed between the two countries, but issues such as the Maitree Express, the Ganges Water Treaty, trade and cultural exchanges should not be allowed to get stuck.
“These are the things of ordinary people," said the High Commissioner, highlighting the importance of keeping the people at the centre.
The High Commissioner said trade restrictions from both sides have to be liberalised. Otherwise, he noted, the people will suffer.
He said there is no need to rush and the political process will take its own course. But the work that concerns ordinary people must continue, Trivedi said.
Trivedi was speaking about the importance of peace and harmony in the region and beyond, referring to the teachings of Lalon Fakir and the traditions of Buddhism and Sufism.
“The world is facing a lot of unrest at this moment. When I talk about the lamp and the lighthouse, I am not talking only about Bangladesh or India; I am talking about the entire subcontinent,” he said.
The High Commissioner said the region's diverse religious and spiritual traditions could contribute to the cause of global peace.
“There is Buddhism here, there is Sufism, and all religions are the same. We can all live together and work together for peace in the world,” Trivedi said.
Expressing optimism about the future, he said positive change might take time but there must be a beginning.
“I have a lot of optimism, and I am absolutely confident. It will take time, but we have to make a good beginning,” he said.
On the political issues between Bangladesh and India, Trivedi said there was no need to repeatedly discuss matters that were already under consideration at the highest level.
“I am completely confident that the Prime Minister of Bangladesh knows what has to be done, where and when. It is his prerogative, and we should leave it to him to decide when he considers it appropriate,” he said.
Trivedi said India would continue to focus on areas that could move forward without being affected by political considerations.
“My responsibility is to ensure that the work does not stop, but I cannot do it alone,” he said.
He stressed the need for the relevant technical committees of the two countries to work on easing trade restrictions and improving economic exchanges.
The High Commissioner attended the inaugural ceremony of the Kabir-Lalon Bhabsangeet Utsav, organised by the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, as special guest.
The event was held at Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Thursday said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first visit to India cannot be a multilateral visit and the government is working on arranging a bilateral visit to India when the timing is conducive.
He stressed that Bangladesh is placing greater emphasis on a bilateral visit by the Prime Minister and discussions.
Kobir said such a bilateral visit will take place when the environment is conducive and mutual respect is maintained. “There is no need to rush things.”
Responding to a question about the renewal of the Ganges Water Treaty, the State Minister said, “Wherever our national interest is involved, we will act with importance and competence. We will prioritise the interests and well-being of our country.”
Kobir said there is no scope for Bangladesh to send a government representative to the BRICS Summit, as Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was not invited to the summit and the invitation was instead extended to the BIMSTEC Chair.
“How shall we go? Has anyone from the Bangladesh government been invited? Our Prime Minister was not invited. Who told you that our Prime Minister was invited? The BIMSTEC Chair was invited. Then why are you asking this question?” he told reporters, ruling out the possibility of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman attending the BRICS Summit.

item.title: Nippon Maru, Cosmo Clock and my Yokohama days
item.description:
In early May 2017, the temperature in Yokohama was mild and comfortable. It was the final month of spring, and I was enjoying my stay in the Japanese port city despite a hectic business schedule. The Asian Development Bank was holding its 50 th annual meeting and I was attending the celebration marking the Bank’s golden jubilee, held at one of the world’s largest integrated convention and exhibition complexes: the Pacific Convention Plaza Yokohama.
This high-angle perspective looks directly down onto the Yokohama Cosmo World amusement park, captured from the 69th-floor observation deck of the Yokohama Landmark Tower Sky Garden. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Located on the waterfront of the futuristic Minato Mirai 21 district, the venue—popularly known as Pacifico Yokohama—is a major tourist attraction in its own right, thanks to its grandeur and striking, maritime-themed architecture that resembles a bivalve seashell and ocean waves.
For several days that May, it became my routine to walk along the beautiful Tokyo Bay area from my hotel near Sakuragicho Station to Pacifico Yokohama. It was a pleasant, 15-minute stroll. Every time I walked past the bustling Queen’s Square—which houses the Minato Mirai Tokyu Square, a major retail and dining destination spanning multiple buildings—my eyes fell upon a beautiful sailing ship docked permanently on the water.
All sails are beautifully unfurled on the Nippon Maru. This is a rare sight, as the historic ship keeps its sails neatly tucked away on a day-to-day basis. This spectacular full-sail display, known as Sōhan Tenpan, happens only 10 to 12 times a year—typically on weekends or public holidays between April and November. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Built by Kawasaki Shipbuilding in Kobe, Japan, the iconic Nippon Maru was launched on January 27, 1930, and served for over five decades as a training vessel, earning the nickname "Swan of the Pacific." A four-masted barque featuring 32 sails, the Nippon Maru is now permanently preserved in a stone dry dock at the Nippon Maru Memorial Park along the western edge of Tokyo Bay.
A barque is a specific type of sailing ship – having three or more masts and special settings of sails – that was highly popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries, particularly for long-distance trade and training.
The historic sail ship Nippon Maru shines bright at night, permanently docked at the Nippon Maru Memorial Park in Minato Mirai 21 district of Yokohama, Japan. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
During its 54 years of active service, Nippon Maru logged over 1.8 million kilometers and trained more than 11,500 navy cadets before retiring in 1984. It also served as an emergency transport and repatriation ship during and after World War II.
Following its retirement, the Yokohama Port Museum began maintaining the ship as a floating exhibit. By a pleasant coincidence, the year I visited Yokohama was the exact year Japan officially designated the Nippon Maru as a National Important Cultural Property.
Sailing ships have many ropes used to operate the sails, and all of them are secured to pins called belaying pins. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
In one of the photos accompanying this feature, readers will notice festive fireworks lighting up the night sky behind the majestic masts. The illuminated numbers "2017" visible in the background celebrate the milestone of its official designation. While strolling around the park grounds is entirely free, visitors can purchase tickets to tour the historic interior decks of the ship and explore the adjacent, semi-underground Yokohama Port Museum.
I loved watching the Nippon Maru during my time in Minato Mirai, but I left with one unfulfilled wish—I never caught a glimpse of it with 29 sails open. Because the "Full-Sail Exhibition" isn't an everyday event, timing is everything. It only happens about 10 to 12 times a year, when a team of roughly 80 volunteers unfurls the sails entirely by hand.
While sailing, the helmsman steers while keeping an eye on the condition of the sails, which is why the steering wheel is located at the very back of the ship. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Beyond the ship, the entire vicinity of Minato Mirai is a tourist paradise. Adjacent to the Nippon Maru Memorial Park is Yokohama Cosmo World, an amusement park where I was captivated by a massive Ferris wheel unlike any I had seen before.
Known as the Cosmo Clock 21, it held the distinction of being the world’s tallest Ferris wheel when it first opened in 1989 at a height of 353 feet. A decade later, it was relocated slightly and rebuilt on a taller platform, raising its total height to 369 feet. While it is no longer the overall tallest, it still holds the unique distinction of being the world's largest Ferris wheel equipped with a clock.
Ship`s Bell. It used to be struck once in every 30 minutes. Traditional nautical watch system revolves around a 4-hour cycle, where time is kept not by looking at a face clock, but by striking a ship`s bell every half-hour. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
During my days in Yokohama, this daily commute between my hotel and Pacifico Yokohama—framed by bustling malls, the World War II-era ship, and the towering Ferris wheel—became a comforting constant. One afternoon, I went up to the 69th floor of the nearby Yokohama Landmark Tower to visit the iconic Sky Garden Observatory.
Completed in 1993, this nearly 1,000-foot skyscraper stood as the tallest building in Japan for over two decades until 2014, and it remains one of the country's tallest structures today. Nursing a relaxing cup of coffee at the Sky Café, I enjoyed a spectacular, 360-degree panoramic view of Yokohama, the sparkling bay, and the Cosmo Clock 21 spinning down below.
This is an image of the ongoing construction of the Dhaka Eye, a massive new observation Ferris wheel taking shape in Central Park of the city’s eastern fringe. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Admiring that giant Ferris wheel in Minato Mirai left a lasting impression on me. Long afterward, the prospect of having one in my own city brought those fond memories of Yokohama rushing back. Today, Dhaka is getting ready for its own first massive Ferris wheel, set to open in the Central Park at the eastern periphery of the city.

item.title: Journalist found dead at Samakal Barisal bureau office
item.description:
Police recovered the hanging body of senior journalist and former Daily Samakal Barisal bureau chief Pulak Chatterjee, 57, from the newspaper’s Barisal bureau office on Friday evening.
The body was recovered from the office on Parara Road in the city.
According to local sources, Pulak Chatterjee had been dismissed from Samakal about three years ago. He was a former general secretary of the Barisal Press Club and had previously worked for Daily Jugantor for many years. He is survived by his wife and a daughter.
Suman Chowdhury, chief staff reporter at Samakal’s Barisal office, said Pulak had a key to the office and often visited it during the day or at night.
“His wife called me in the afternoon and said he was not answering his phone. When I came to the office in the evening, I found the door locked from inside. Looking through a gap, I saw him hanging with a noose around his neck. I immediately informed the police,” he said.
Police later broke open the door and recovered the body.
Pulak had most recently served as Samakal’s Barisal bureau chief. He had reportedly been mentally distressed since losing his job at the newspaper about three years ago.
Al Mamun-ul Islam, officer-in-charge of Barisal Kotwali Model Police Station, said police initially suspected suicide.
“The exact cause of death will be known after the autopsy report,” he said.

item.title: Padma erosion washes away three schools in Bagha, 20,000 people stranded
item.description:
Erosion by the Padma River has washed away three government primary schools in Bagha upazila of Rajshahi, forcing the authorities concerned to relocate school materials and suspend classes.
The affected schools are Palashi Fatepur, Atarpara and Chaumadia government primary schools in Chakrajapur union.
Meanwhile, around 20,000 people from 1,200 families in 15 riverine chars, including Chakrajapur, Kalidaskhali, Laxminagar, Dadpur, Nich Palashi, Palashi Fatepur, Atarpara, Chaumadia and Diyar Kadimpur, have been stranded by rising water. More than 100 houses and several mosques have also been washed away by the river.
Locals said the Padma began rising abruptly on September 1, triggering severe erosion in the chars. The three schools were gradually threatened by the advancing river before being washed away. Their furniture and other materials were moved to safer locations, but classes remain suspended.
Abdur Rahman, a former member of Ward 2 of Chakrajapur union parishad, confirmed the developments on Thursday.
Shafiqul Islam, headteacher of Atarpara Government Primary School, said the school had been repeatedly relocated as the river continued to erode the char. “We would see the school standing one day and find it gone the next. Eventually, it was washed away while we were moving its belongings,” he said.
The school has 85 students and three teachers. Following instructions from the Bagha upazila executive officer, school materials were being removed when the building was finally swallowed by the river around noon on Wednesday.
Soleman Molla, a resident of Chaumadia char, said the continued rise in the Padma's water level had created serious difficulties for residents, particularly in protecting their livestock.
Sohail Rana, acting headteacher of Chaumadia Government Primary School, said there was no safe way to reach the school, so classes had been suspended. The school has 91 students and three teachers.
Bagha Upazila Nirbahi Officer Taqi Faisal Talukdar said he had visited the erosion-hit areas and schools and arranged for school materials to be moved from Atarpara.
“The matter has been reported to the higher authorities. Steps are also being taken to provide assistance to people stranded by the rising water,” he said.

item.title: Jamaat not to be lenient to NCP in Dhaka’s 2 city corporations
item.description:
Jamaat-e-Islami is unwilling to concede ground to the National Citizen Party (NCP) in the upcoming mayoral elections for Dhaka's two city corporations.

Although the two parties allied for the national parliamentary election, both are now preparing to field separate mayoral candidates this time. Other partners within the 11-party alliance will also nominate candidates based on their organisational strength.

However, despite competing against each other in local body elections, leaders of these political parties maintain that they will preserve their political unity and conduct joint programmes.

According to relevant sources, a policy decision has been taken by the 11-party alliance to contest all tiers of local government elections independently, not just the two Dhaka city corporations.

This decision reflects the reality that local elections are not conducted under party symbols, as well as local-level candidate selection dynamics.

Nevertheless, if coalition partners reach a local consensus to field a single joint candidate in any specific area, the central leadership will not object.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on Friday, Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar stated that the 11-party alliance was originally formed around the national parliamentary elections. During a meeting of top leaders from the member parties, it was decided that each entity would contest local government elections independently.

He noted that the NCP has decided to field its own candidates in Dhaka's two cities and that other coalition partners with sufficient organisational capacity are equally free to nominate candidates.

Mia Golam Porwar added that this decision applies to all city corporation elections across the country, not merely Dhaka. Since the elections will not feature party symbols, there is no scope for alliance-based vote-sharing. Voters, he emphasised, will elect qualified candidates based on merit.

The Jamaat leaders indicated that local district and upazila leaders are currently announcing candidates' names. By their estimates, around 70 to 75 per cent of candidate announcements have already been completed. City corporation candidates are also largely finalised, though official announcements have not yet been made.

Nominations for all local government tiers, including city corporations, will be formally announced simultaneously from the party's central headquarters.

According to Jamaat sources, Mohammad Salim Uddin, Ameer of the party's Dhaka City North branch, has been initially nominated as the Mayoral candidate in Dhaka North City Corporation, while Md Abu Shadik (Shadik Kayem), Vice President of the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (DUCSU), has been nominated for Dhaka South.

Salim Uddin has already commenced grassroots campaign activities, while Shadik Kayem has also stepped up his outreach efforts.

Meanwhile, NCP sources reveal that party spokesperson Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain is set to contest in Dhaka North, while Chief Coordinator Nasiruddin Patwary will run in Dhaka South. However, the NCP has yet to make an official announcement. It is understood that the NCP is also preparing to field individual candidates across other local government levels.

Another member of the 11-party alliance, Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis, is likewise preparing to nominate candidates in both Dhaka city corporations. Maulana Hasan Junaid, the party's Publicity Secretary and Media Coordinator, informed Prothom Alo yesterday that they currently have four potential candidates across the two cities, and two final selections will be made following a screening process.

The AB Party will also field candidates in the two Dhaka cities and other city corporations, confirmed party Chairman Mojibur Rahman Manju. Speaking to Prothom Alo yesterday, he stated that those wishing to contest will receive party endorsement, and candidates will be fielded across other local government levels according to organisational capacity.

However, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), another partner in the 11-party alliance, has not yet finalised its strategy. LDP Acting Secretary General Billal Hossain Miaji told Prothom Alo that the party president and presidium members would discuss the matter before arriving at a decision.

Despite the central directive to field separate candidates, room remains for local-level compromises among coalition partners. Hamidur Rahman Azad, Coordinator of the 11-party alliance and Assistant Secretary General of Jamaat-e-Islami, told Prothom Alo yesterday that no centralised seat-sharing agreements will take place for local body elections. Parties will make their own preparations; however, if local units reach mutual understandings, the central leadership will not intervene.

Hamidur Rahman Azad also urged the government and the election commission to promptly announce the schedule for local government elections.

A top NCP leader, speaking to Prothom Alo yesterday evening on condition of anonymity, confirmed that the NCP would contest independently.

The leader noted that in the absence of party symbols, individual candidate appeal would take precedence over party affiliation, meaning local unity would remain largely unaffected at the ballot box.

Jamaat central leaders, however, believe there is limited room for local-level seat sharing, asserting that Jamaat candidates will command an advantage in most areas based on eligibility and public recognition.

Electoral separation, joint political action

Sources from both Jamaat and the NCP emphasised that while they will field separate candidates in local elections, they intend to preserve their overarching political coalition. The parties plan to host joint movement programmes on matters of public interest, including the implementation of the national referendum outcome, as well as ongoing power and gas crises.

Insiders noted that measures will be taken to coordinate among alliance candidates to prevent inter-party friction on the ground. Should there be non-cooperation from the election commission or government authorities, or attempts to exert undue influence in favour of ruling party candidates, the alliance partners will launch unified protests.

Jamaat Assistant Secretary General Abdul Halim told Prothom Alo that while electoral consensus will not exist at the local government level, political understanding will remain intact.

According to him, field-level movement programmes will be conducted jointly, and if the ruling party attempts to manipulate the elections, the 11-party alliance will register a united resistance.

item.title: New rules on animal slaughter, abattoirs shut down and the despair of Firoz
item.description:
Firoz Alam had never imagined such hard times would come into his life. Just a few months ago, his shop in Shibpur, Howrah, saw a good footfall of customers. Back then, eight to ten kilograms of meat were easily sold every day. However, the situation changed almost overnight after the elections.

With slaughterhouses closed following a government directive, his two-generation-old business is now on the verge of collapse. Firoz faces a tough situation just trying to provide two meals a day for his family, which includes his wife, elderly mother and three children.

Crossing the Second Hooghly Bridge in West Bengal, India, near the Bataitala market, a tea-stall owner pointed out Firoz's shop upon simply hearing his name in front of the Dinabandhu Andrews Institution. Taking the road to the left from the Kazipara intersection and moving forward a bit, a young man in his thirties came forward with a smile at the entrance of a narrow alley.

Two and a half decades ago, his father used to sell meat in a tiny shop in this very alley. Firoz took over the shop five years ago after his father's death. His maternal uncle sits in the adjacent shop. Rather than business rivalry, they have always helped each other.

Firoz said, "We take turns bringing meat from the Tikiapara slaughterhouse. Large wholesale shops are lined up there. Meat is supplied to hotels and restaurants every day from there. But since the slaughterhouse closed, not all shops are in a position to open every day now."

After the BJP came to power in West Bengal, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari's government issued a new directive in early May imposing strict conditions on cattle slaughter. Since then, an unprecedented financial and social crisis has emerged surrounding the beef market in the state. Following the imposition of the new directives and rules, the decision to make health check-up certificates mandatory for cattle at slaughterhouses has had a direct impact on the entire meat supply chain.

Firoz Alam, a meat seller, West Bengal, IndiaWe used to bring meat from the Tikiapara slaughterhouse. But the slaughterhouse has been closed for almost a month. Nothing clear has been said about when it will reopen. To keep the shop running, meat has to be brought through roundabout ways, which comes at a steep price for various reasons. Consequently, the resulting price of meat is making it difficult for middle-class and poor customers to buy.

According to the directive, slaughtering cattle other than those over 14 years of age, or those completely incapable of physical labour and breeding, is prohibited. The responsibility of conducting health check-ups of the animals and issuing clearance certificates in this regard has been jointly assigned to the chairman of the respective municipality or the president of the panchayat samiti, along with a government-approved veterinary surgeon.

As a result of this administrative complexity and the strict enforcement of rules, the supply of cattle to animal slaughter centers in various parts of the state, including the government slaughterhouse in the Tangra area of Kolkata, has hit rock bottom.

Employees, speaking on condition of anonymity, reported that since the introduction of the new restrictions, more than half of the animals brought for slaughter have had to be turned back as they failed to obtain health clearances. Consequently, the daily supply of meat in the market has taken a hit.

Incidentally, according to the fifth National Family Health Survey, West Bengal ranks second on the list of India's most non-vegetarian states. Various types of fish, meat and eggs are included in the daily diet of about 98.55 per cent of the people in this state. An average family tends to spend about 20 per cent of their monthly expenses on meat and fish. The survey also reported that the consumption of eggs and animal protein in the state has increased by about 17 per cent over the last five years.

Recently, a Hindu religious leader from another state criticised Bengalis for eating non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja, sparking intense public outrage against him. Right before the upcoming festive season, both buyers and sellers are worried as slaughterhouses remain non-operational due to the government directive. Meanwhile, rumors on social media about meat shops being closed during Devipaksha for Navaratri have caused an uproar. However, the state administration has thus far denied issuing any such notification.

Small-scale meat sellers, butchers and retail traders at local markets have taken the biggest hit due to the suspension of animal slaughter. Small meat shops that have been operating for decades in the markets of Kolkata, Howrah and surrounding districts are facing extreme uncertainty. For small traders, buying cattle for meat and the complex process of gathering administrative clearances have become the biggest problems. Buying animals from peripheral areas and bringing them to the city, gathering their correct age and health-related certificates and taking them to designated municipal slaughterhouses—this entire process multiplies both time and costs, concerned individuals claim.

Regarding this, Firoz Alam, a meat seller in the Kazipara area of Howrah, said, "We used to bring meat from the Tikiapara slaughterhouse. But the slaughterhouse has been closed for almost a month. Nothing clear has been said about when it will reopen. To keep the shop running, meat has to be brought through roundabout ways, which comes at a steep price for various reasons. Consequently, the resulting price of meat is making it difficult for middle-class and poor customers to buy."

Munabbar Ali, another meat seller in Howrah, said that due to strictness at government slaughterhouses, animals are being slaughtered illegally to meet market demand. He claims that with the Tikiapara slaughterhouse currently closed, cows and buffaloes are being slaughtered while evading the administration's vigilance in multiple locations in Arambagh, Uluberia, Duttapukur and Barasat.

Such animal slaughter is usually carried out in open fields and crop fields outside populated areas in the early morning. However, before that, everything is settled by speaking with the local panchayat authorities and a section of the law enforcement forces, definitely through financial transactions. Sellers transport that meat from these makeshift slaughterhouses to their shops in pickup vans or small trucks covered with tarpaulin. On the way, traffic police on the roads have to be paid ten to twelve thousand rupees per vehicle. In addition, he claims that the local police station has to be regularly kept ‘satisfied’ to get ‘approval’ to sell beef and buffalo meat in the area.

Shamser Alam, local trader, West Bengal, India The government slaughterhouse is closed. In the meantime, although it was said it would reopen twice, it ultimately didn't happen. I don't know how much longer I can keep the shop open by struggling like this.

Besides having to buy products at higher rates from outside government slaughterhouses, meeting these extra costs has caused the price of meat to increase in just three to four months. Firoz says, "Even before the last Eid, beef was sold at Rs 250 per kg. But since the slaughterhouse closed, its price has now risen to Rs 350-360 per kg." For the same reason, along with beef, buffalo meat is also being sold at a higher price.

Like Firoz and Munabbar, Idris Ali, a meat seller in Park Circus, is on the verge of closing his business due to the government ban. Idris, who has been in this profession for nearly a dozen years, has never faced such a situation before. However, he does not believe the business of slaughtering animals outside authorized slaughterhouses will last long.

Meanwhile, the police have launched regular search operations and are conducting arrests with the aim of shutting down illegal slaughterhouses. For this reason, meat supply shortages are occurring frequently. Consequently, several low-capital sellers are losing their investments and being forced to wind up their businesses overnight, a shop owner in Topsia said. For the same reason, sellers are being forced to keep their meat shops closed one after another in the historic New Market in the Dharmatala area of Kolkata.

Due to this massive supply shortage, several popular restaurants in the city have been forced to remove many of their popular beef dishes. Due to a lack of meat supply, people are being disappointed when ordering beef rolls, beef biryani or beef steaks at many traditional restaurants like Nizams, Zam Zam, Olypub or Mocambo.

Cooking mutton or chicken dishes as alternatives is not bringing much relief, claims a restaurant owner in the Beckbagan area. To manage the situation in the dining halls of five-star hotels, beef has to be bought online at steep prices, an official in charge of the kitchen at a popular hotel in the Alipore area stated. However, hotel authorities are anxious about how long it will be possible to keep beef dishes on the menu this way.

On the other hand, in several roadside shops in central Kolkata, kebabs, rezala, tikiya, bhuna, etc. are being prepared using buffalo meat as an alternative to beef, although a popular food vlogger from Dum Dum complained that it doesn't bring out the taste like beef. He claims that taking advantage of this, several restaurants on online platforms are freely passing off 'buff', meaning buffalo meat as beef.

The local police station has to be regularly kept ‘satisfied’ to get ‘approval’ to sell beef and buffalo meat in the area.

The impact of such a beef crisis has not only affected humans. It has also put the carnivorous residents of the Alipore Zoo, such as tigers, lions and leopards, in trouble. With the slaughter of buffaloes and other cattle halted or limited at the Tangra slaughterhouse, the daily feed for those animals has been hit.

As companies supplying buffalo meat to the zoo failed to renew their registration and maintain supply, zoo authorities are being forced to buy goat meat at four times the price to feed the carnivorous animals. Consequently, the allocated budget for food at the government zoo has skyrocketed overnight, which has ultimately created additional financial pressure at the administrative level.

Due to the closure of slaughterhouses by government order, the struggle of daily life has become difficult for many others associated with it, besides meat sellers. That list includes small traders, the vast majority of whom are Hindu.They ran their households by taking loans from moneylenders to buy and raise calves and then selling the adult cattle.

Even before the last Eid, beef was sold at Rs 250 per kg. But since the slaughterhouse closed, its price has now risen to Rs 350-360 per kg.

Following the imposition of conditions on animal slaughter through the government notice, instead of profits, the burden of debt has fallen on their shoulders. The crisis has deepened further due to the collapse of the rural economy associated with the buying and selling of cattle. Farmers in rural areas who used to sell old or useless cattle to buy new ones or raise money for family needs are also not finding buyers now.

As the buying and selling of cattle in markets has decreased, it has also impacted the rural economy. Added to this is a severe shortage of raw materials in the leather industry and tanneries. As a result, many small-scale traders who collect the skins of dead animals from slaughterhouses and supply them to tanneries are suffering losses.

A seller in Tikiapara lamented that no ray of hope has been seen so far regarding how to resolve the difficult problem faced by meat outlets, restaurants, and various associated businesses as a result of the government ban. "The government slaughterhouse is closed. In the meantime, although it was said it would reopen twice, it ultimately didn't happen. I don't know how much longer I can keep the shop open by struggling like this," said local trader Shamser Alam. Firoz from Kazipara sighed and said, "Perhaps this time there will be no other way left but to pull a rickshaw."

item.title: US marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
item.description:
US-ATTACKS-9/11-ANNIVERSARY-TRUMP

The United States on Friday commemorated the 25th anniversary of the devastating 11 September 2001 attacks with a poignant ceremony in New York marked by President Donald Trump's absence and searing criticism from victims' relatives.

In an unusual move, Trump paid his respects at the Pentagon, not the event in New York, where hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and most of the 2,977 victims were killed, upending the global status quo.

The Republican billionaire sought to link the "war on terror" that followed 9/11, which sparked years of US involvement in Middle East wars, with his current conflict in Iran.

"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today," Trump said.

"We don't have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win."

But several bereaved family members who read out the names of those killed criticized Saudi Arabia and US leaders' closeness to the kingdom.

'We have no justice'

Terry Strada, whose husband Tom Strada died in the Twin Towers, unleashed a stinging attack on Riyadh, accusing it of complicity in the attacks, and denouncing former presidents who were in attendance.

"You are missed more with each year that passes, but how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?" she said.

The 11 September 2001 attacks were carried out by mostly Saudi hijackers and orchestrated by Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, a wealthy Saudi.

"For 25 years, administration after administration -- including leaders in front of us here today -- chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with a 9/11 family," Strada said, calling for action from the absent Trump.

In New York, Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the Big Apple's first Muslim leader, attended the Ground Zero event despite a campaign urging him to stay away.

That effort was spearheaded by the right-wing New York Post newspaper and former mayor and Trump ally Rudy Giuliani, who led the city through the crisis and was also present on Friday.

The petition gathered more than 100,000 signatures.

A small anti-Islam protest gathered at City Hall and marched towards Ground Zero, flanked by a heavy police presence and counter-protesters.

Mamdani won plaudits for revealing thousands of documents showing what city officials knew about toxicity levels of the air in Lower Manhattan following the attacks.

After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers from which thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today.

The CIA also declassified and published dozens of 9/11-related presidential intelligence briefs to coincide with the 25th anniversary.

'New York did recover'

Nineteen Al-Qaeda operatives hijacked four airliners on the nearly cloudless autumn day in 2001.

Two of the jets slammed into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, causing the iconic skyscrapers to collapse.

A third plane struck the Pentagon, while a fourth -- believed to have been aiming for Congress or the White House -- crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back.

Some 100 million Americans have been born since or are too young to remember the traumatic day.

Sophia Rotunno, 58, recalls watching the first tower fall with colleagues back in 2001, and also remembers helping those affected in the aftermath.

"All we could do is support them, and be there for when they went to memorials, or be there for when they came home, and hug them, and pray for them," she said.

"It was a hard time for everybody afterward -- and New York did recover."

Al-Qaeda meanwhile marked the anniversary by releasing a video showing images of the late Bin Laden and his son Hamza, who Trump said in 2019 had also been killed.
