item.title: Who will pay for the climate crisis?
item.description:
NEPAL-FLOODS/

Nepal has demanded climate compensation after the recent devastating landslides and floods that killed thousands and caused widespread damage. The question that Nepal has raised by demanding compensation from major emitters like the United States, India, and China is not unique to Nepal. Rather, it is one of the world’s biggest justice questions: who will ultimately pay for the damage caused by climate change?

To find the answer to this question, we need to look back. Since the Industrial Revolution, much of the world’s economic growth has been based on coal, oil, and gas. These fuels have fueled unprecedented prosperity in the economies, urbanization, and lifestyles of industrialised countries. But the environmental costs of that prosperity are not just on their shoulders.

Global warming is increasing, sea levels are rising, rainfall patterns are changing, cyclones and heat waves are intensifying, droughts are getting longer in some places, and the risk of floods and landslides is increasing in others. And the biggest impact of all this is often falling on countries that have played a relatively small role in creating this crisis.

This is where the biggest paradox of climate change lies. The countries or populations that have contributed the least to global warming often suffer the most. A coastal farmer in Bangladesh, a small farmer in Africa, or a family in a remote village in the Himalayas did not make the decision to join the global carbon economy. But they are paying the price of climate change with their lives and livelihoods.

So the question arises, is this just bad luck, or is it a matter of responsibility?

This is where the concept of climate justice comes into play. Not all countries are equally responsible for the climate crisis, nor are all countries equally affected. As a result, the argument that everyone should be equally responsible for the solution does not stand the test of fairness.

Countries that have achieved economic prosperity by emitting large amounts of greenhouse gases for a long time cannot be limited to reducing emissions in the future. They must also face the question of taking responsibility for a part of the damage caused today due to those past emissions.

There is a debate over the word ‘compensation’. Many in developed countries want to see climate finance as a continuation of development aid. On the other hand, affected countries argue that getting money for damage they did not cause due to the climate crisis is not kindness. It should be part of a fair international system.

The difference between the two positions is very important. Aid usually depends on the goodwill of the donor. But compensation depends on liability. When asking for aid, the poor country is a beneficiary; but when it demands fair compensation, it speaks of its rights. This change in language is very important in climate politics.

Of course, there is a hard reality here. It is not possible to hold any specific country responsible for the entire damage of every flood, cyclone or landslide in the world. In addition to climate change, local topography, deforestation, unplanned urbanization, weak infrastructure or a lack of disaster management can also make a disaster more severe.  Therefore, an effective compensation system should not be based on emotions, but on scientific evidence, historical emissions, current emissions, economic viability and the scale of damage.

But this complexity does not negate the need for compensation. On the contrary, it shows that we need a more fair and effective international system.

The world is already talking about ‘Loss and Damage’. The UN climate process has decided to create a fund for this. This is undoubtedly an important step forward. But creating a fund is not the same as ensuring sufficient money compared to the need.

This is the major weakness of the current system. The scale of damage from the climate crisis is increasing rapidly, while compensation money still depends largely on voluntary commitments and political will. Uncertain and inadequate financing cannot be a sustainable solution to the damage of a crisis that has accumulated over decades and whose effects will continue for decades to come.

The bigger question is, where will this money come from?

Relying solely on the national budgets of developed countries will be difficult to meet in the long term. Proposals such as a global levy on the excess profits of the fossil fuel industry, certain types of charges on international aviation and shipping, mandatory contributions from high-emitting countries, or creating new sources of finance through the international financial system could be seriously considered for climate compensation. It is not unreasonable to create a link between an economy that has long benefited from its dependence on fossil fuels and an economy that has benefited from climate damage.

Another issue is whether loss-and-damage finance should come in the form of loans. On paper, a loan may count as climate finance. But from the perspective of justice, the picture is very different. If a country that has suffered economic losses due to floods, cyclones, or rising sea levels has to borrow again to deal with those losses, the burden of the loss is simply shifted from the present to the future.  Therefore, financing for loss and damage needs to be as grant-based and predictable as possible.

The greatest injustice of the climate crisis may not simply be that some people are losing their homes, land and livelihoods. It may be that those who contributed least to creating the crisis are being asked to pay the highest price for it.

Here, the question of the responsibility of the developed world is even clearer. Just as it is not right to simply claim that the development of industrialized countries is not entirely due to climate change, it is also not consistent with reality to deny the role of their historical emissions. Today''s climate crisis is not the result of any one year's emissions; it is the result of accumulated emissions over many decades. Therefore, determining responsibility only by looking at current emissions leaves out a large part of history.

At the same time, the reality of the current world must be acknowledged. Countries like China and India are now among the world's largest emitters, although their historical responsibility and per capita emissions are not the same as those of developed Western countries. As a result, a future climate compensation system cannot be stuck in a simple division of ''West vs. the rest of the world''. Those with greater historical responsibility, higher current emissions, and greater economic capacity must take proportionately greater responsibility.

That is, the basis of climate compensation should be justice, not revenge.
Another important aspect of this justice is where the money will go. The responsibility does not end when money is deposited in international funds. If money is also stuck in the bureaucratic structures of the affected country, or if the needs of local people are neglected in the name of large infrastructure projects, then that funding will lose its original purpose.

The invisible cost of climate change: Bangladesh's non-economic losses

The ultimate beneficiaries of climate compensation must be the people who are actually suffering—coastal farmers, landless families in river erosion, displaced people, small-scale fishers, agricultural workers, and communities whose livelihoods have been lost due to climate change.
This debate is therefore particularly important for Bangladesh.

We have long been known as one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries. Although our emissions are very small compared to the global crisis, the impact of climate change on our development, agriculture, water, coastal life, and human migration is becoming increasingly visible. As a result, climate financing for Bangladesh is not just another matter of international aid; it is a question of future development and justice.

However, we also need to be careful about one thing. Demanding compensation alone is not enough. What the international framework for compensation will be, what damage will be considered compensable, how liability will be scientifically determined, how the money will be distributed, and how it will reach local people—these are questions that countries like Bangladesh need to take a stronger stance on.

Much of the discussion on climate change has been about how to prevent future disasters. Then came the question of how to adapt people to those changes. Now comes the more difficult question—who will pay for the damage that has already been done?

The answer to this question is not just a question of money. It is also a question of history. It is a question of development models. It is a question of power. And most of all, it is a question of justice.

Nepal’s recent claim has only brought that question to the fore. But the question is much bigger than Nepal. As the number and scale of climate disasters increase in the coming days, the world will have to decide—will we keep climate-affected countries dependent on sympathy and relief, or will we accept their losses as part of a just international obligation?

Climate change does not respect national borders. Its consequences do not stop at the borders of the countries least responsible for causing it. If the benefits of carbon-intensive development have been accumulated disproportionately in one part of the world while its costs are increasingly borne elsewhere, then the international system must find a fairer way to share those costs.

The greatest injustice of the climate crisis may not simply be that some people are losing their homes, land and livelihoods. It may be that those who contributed least to creating the crisis are being asked to pay the highest price for it.

* Atia Ibnat Rifah, and Azizul Hakim Rakib are postrgaduate students at the Department of International Relations, University of Rajshahi. item.title: Protecting the hand that hurts
item.description:
Picture a courtroom in Bangladesh. A woman is sitting on a bench, hiding her bruises, and waiting to testify against her own husband who beats her mercilessly.
When her name is called, she suddenly changes her original story, fervently trying to withdraw the case and convince the magistrate that her injuries were rather the result of an accident.
Outside the courtroom, her mother-in-law is standing, waiting for her to take her to the same house, the same husband, and the same violence.
This is not a rare scenario in Bangladesh’s family courts or police stations; rather, it is a pattern so common here that oftentimes the police or the court shows reluctance to even register cases of domestic violence.
Why do these women, despite years of abuse, try to protect their abusers?
To answer this question, let us travel 53 years into the past.
In 1973, four employees (three women and one man) of Kreditbanken Bank in Stockholm were taken hostage by two robbers for six days.
By the time the police were able to free them, they had grown protective of their captors, refusing to testify against the perpetrators and instead raising money for their legal defense.
Psychiatrists called this condition Stockholm Syndrome; a survival response where the victim develops sympathy, even loyalty toward the abuser who controls their fear.
Similarly, among women who are victims of abuse, a long period of intimate violence and torture produces Stockholm Syndrome in the form of fierce trauma bonding, which leads to an unintentional instinct to protect their abuser from consequences of their own.
In Bangladesh’s household scenario, this trauma bond rarely announces itself as a pathology; rather, it looks like a housewife telling her neighbours that the bruises on her face are from an accidental fall down the stairs, a mother telling her daughter to call the injuries on her body marks of a self-inflicted accident, or a young wife defending her husband’s violence as occasional outbursts of anger.
According to analysts, the main reasons for South Asian women experiencing Stockholm Syndrome are financial dependency, fear of social stigma, patriarchal society, and a conviction that suffering silently is a form of loyalty and a badge of honour for women. A woman's own family often supports this idea of protecting the abusive husband at any cost.
This is akin to the boiling-frog pattern, where researchers illustrate that when abuse towards a woman increases gradually, she can lose the ability or the willingness to protect herself or remove herself from the situation.
Based on the irrational belief that the world cannot offer her a better alternative than what she already has, she thus ends up subconsciously developing instincts to protect her abusive partner.
To make things worse, the Domestic Violence Act (2010) in Bangladesh every so often clashes head-on with the involuntary, deep state of self-preservation in women who have been conditioned to defend their abusers.
As a result, police, often reluctantly, send complaints back for domestic violence matters to be settled “domestically.”
Millions of women enable their partners to continue abusing them throughout their relationships. However, putting the onus of standing up to violence on the victims themselves is easy but, by no means, fair.
Instead, we need to ask the difficult questions here.
Why, after all, do the abused women enable their abusers? And why do they keep protecting these sadist oppressors?
A quick glance at these ill-fated women’s formative years will tell you why.
Since their early days, many women see their mothers silently suffer physical and mental torture, verbal assault, and various other forms of hostility in their own house.
These women keep hearing from their family, neighbours, relatives, and everyone else in society that domestic disputes are normal between married couples, that “purush manush ektu emoni hoy, meye der manay nite hoy” (men will be men and women need to adjust), that a woman’s real house is her husband’s house, and that a good wife should prioritize her family honour and endure her husband’s maltreatment at any cost.
The mass media these women become exposed to during the developmental period further normalizes and even glamorizes violence against women.
Many movies, dramas, and even cartoons typically characterize women as damsels in distress and men as their saviors, romanticizing toxic relationships and portraying physical violence as a sign of passionate love.
Essentially, when a woman is repetitively told that she is a nobody without her husband, the narrative gets fixated in her mind.
Sometimes this narrative can become so noxious that women even end up becoming complicit in their husbands’ crimes. In the brutal Ramisa rape and murder case, for instance, the wife of the offender actively took part in the atrocity.
While this woman’s crimes are unforgivable, have we ever stopped to think that perhaps it was Stockholm Syndrome that made her feel compelled to protect her husband?
What can be done to save these women from themselves? Do we really believe that only enforcing stricter laws against domestic violence, getting more women educated, or helping women become financially independent will solve the issue?
Admittedly, a combined effort from all these fronts will likely improve the situation to a certain extent. However, until and unless our society recalibrates its views on domestic violence and stops telling women to adjust, accept, and adapt, women will continue to protect the very hand that hurts them.
Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at BRAC Business School and Faizah Zahin is an English and Humanities student, BRAC University.

item.title: On the road again
item.description:
My sister and her retired husband have benefited from forms of support that would be unimaginable in many countries. Assistance with household tasks, social support, and allied health services can help older people and people with disabilities remain at home and maintain a degree of independence.
Australia's aged-care system formally includes services such as social work and physiotherapy among the forms of support that can be provided in home and community settings.
Australia's relatively high wages are another part of this social model. As of July 2026, the national minimum wage is A$26.44 an hour, or A$1,004.90 for a 38-hour week,
Singapore provides another fascinating example.
I spent a couple of weeks there and was struck by what highly educated, pragmatic, and institutionally minded leadership can accomplish when it is combined with administrative competence and a long-term vision.
I visited a school whose principal had become something of a legendary figure. He had grown up poor and had been supported by teachers from religious communities different from his own. His life story was therefore a personal testament to the possibilities of education and merit.
He also played an important role in promoting the recognition of South Asian languages in Singapore's educational system.
Singapore's mother-tongue policy is particularly interesting in this respect. Alongside the country's four official mother tongues -- English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, and Tamil -- students who meet the relevant criteria can study non-Tamil Indian languages, including Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Punjabi, and Urdu.
The principal told me about an encounter he had with Lee Kuan Yew. He explained that he had argued for the importance of allowing children to maintain a connection with their mother tongue. Lee understood the argument and gave his support.
The principal proudly showed me a copy of the letter, now framed and displayed on the wall of his office.
The episode stayed with me because it illustrated something larger than language policy. A country's development is not simply a matter of GDP, technology, or infrastructure. It is also about whether its leaders understand the importance of education, culture, language, and human dignity.
Travel in the global age may no longer give us the same sense of discovering an unknown world that it once did.
Before the internet, arriving in a distant country could mean entering a world about which we knew very little. Today, Google, YouTube, social media, and satellite television have brought much of the world into our living rooms.
But travel has not become irrelevant. Quite the opposite.
Travel allows us to test what we think we know against what actually exists. It introduces us to people whose lives cannot be reduced to statistics.
It allows us to see institutions at work rather than merely read about them. And occasionally, it offers an insight that is difficult to obtain from books or screens.
In Zadar, the sea itself became an orchestra.
In Croatia, I saw how a small country takes education and sport seriously.
Among Bangladeshi migrants, I was reminded of the distance that can exist between a country's citizens and the people who govern them.
In Australia, I saw how democratic institutions and a welfare state can become part of everyday life.
And in Singapore, I was reminded of the transformative possibilities of education and leadership.
Perhaps, then, the real purpose of travel is not to see places. It is to see societies.
These experiences have left me with one broader thought.
Countries do not develop simply because they possess natural resources, favourable geography, or large populations.
Nor does economic growth automatically produce a just, prosperous, or cohesive society.
Institutions have to be built, maintained, and protected. Schools must function. Public officials must do their jobs. Governments must think beyond the next election. And leaders must understand that public office is a responsibility, not a private entitlement.
Education matters enormously because educated leaders are more likely to understand the complexity of modern societies, appreciate evidence, learn from experience, and recognize the importance of institutions.
But education by itself is not enough. An educated person without integrity can become more dangerous, not less.
Knowledge must be accompanied by honesty, competence, humility, and a commitment to the public good.
The examples I encountered on the road -- from Croatia to Australia to Singapore -- are obviously very different, and none should be romanticized. Every society has its contradictions, inequalities, and failures.
Yet they illustrate a common principle: Development depends not only on resources and policies but on the quality of institutions and the people entrusted with them.
A country needs leaders who are educated enough to understand the world, honest enough to resist corruption, competent enough to turn ideas into institutions, and humble enough to listen to ordinary citizens.
Perhaps that is the most important lesson of travel.
The distance between countries is no longer very great. We can cross it in hours.
But the distance between good governance and bad governance, between competent leadership and incompetence, between public service and self-service, can determine the fate of an entire generation.
And that distance is not measured in kilometres.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Ensuring the right to healthcare
item.description:
Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain’s declaration that either he or irregularities in hospitals will remain is certainly a strong statement, but the circumstances under which he said so are deeply concerning.
A surprise inspection of Mugda Medical College Hospital was conducted, where the complaints being investigated were unfortunately found to be true -- including that of patients being sent to outside diagnostic centres, despite the hospital having facilities to conduct the required tests.
This is just one example of what is undoubtedly a gross neglect of people's right to healthcare.
Government hospitals are meant to provide accessible healthcare to those who cannot afford expensive private treatment. When patients are directed elsewhere for services that are already available within public facilities, they are not only being made to spend more money, but may also be exposed to unnecessary additional steps and other irregular practices.
The minister also heard complaints about lifts not operating regularly, forcing patients and their relatives to struggle between floors. Such seemingly basic failures can become serious problems for elderly, sick, and disabled patients.
However, impromptu inspections and strong statements can only take us so far. What matters now is what actions are truly taken.
To that end, those responsible for irregularities must be identified and held accountable, while systems should be put in place to ensure such practices cannot simply return once the spotlight moves elsewhere.
This should also be a nationwide effort. If irregularities exist in one government hospital, there is every reason to examine whether similar problems exist elsewhere.
Regular unannounced inspections, transparent complaint mechanisms, proper monitoring of diagnostic services, and consequences for those abusing public facilities can help restore confidence in the system.
Our public hospitals serve millions, often under difficult circumstances. They deserve better management, stronger oversight, and greater accountability.
The minister has made his position clear. Now the health sector needs to see to it that his position is translated into lasting action.

item.title: Keeping the city clean
item.description:
It is disconcerting that in Dhaka, a city that generates more than 7,000 tons of waste every day, finding a public bin is still challenging -- a basic gap in public infrastructure that should no longer be acceptable.
The absence of bins makes responsible waste disposal unnecessarily difficult. A pedestrian carrying disposables accumulated through daily activities should not have to walk for kilometres to find somewhere to dispose of them.
While this inconvenience certainly cannot excuse littering, it does highlight the responsibility of the city corporations to provide practical facilities that make good behaviour possible.
There have been attempts before. In 2016, more than 11,000 mini bins were installed across Dhaka, but most disappeared within about a year because of theft and inadequate monitoring.
The fact that the capital is facing essentially the same problem a decade later shows that simply installing bins is not enough.
The current plan by Dhaka South City Corporation to install 2,000 heavier, more durable bins is therefore welcome -- but this time, the authorities must also ensure proper placement, regular maintenance, monitoring, and timely waste collection.
Dhaka North City Corporation, meanwhile, should move quickly to finalize a dedicated roadside-bin program instead of leaving pedestrians without convenient disposal options.
At the same time, public responsibility cannot be overlooked. Bins are useful only when people actually use them, and damaging or stealing public facilities only makes an already difficult problem much worse. Littering should not become the default simply because facilities are inadequate.
Ultimately, this is about more than waste management. Public services should be designed around the everyday needs of citizens, while citizens must also take responsibility for protecting and using those services properly. A cleaner Dhaka will require both.
The city corporations must provide the infrastructure and accountability, and the public must do its part too. Only then can keeping Dhaka clean become a shared responsibility rather than an endless struggle.

item.title: ‘CA’ disclaimer sparks customer row at 'Live Shopping' in Mirpur
item.description:
A clothing and accessory shop named “Live Shopping” near Pallabi Metro Station in Dhaka’s Mirpur was closed on Friday afternoon following an altercation between customers and sellers over promotional offer terms.
The incident took place on the fifth floor of the Modern Convention Hall building adjacent to Pallabi Metro Station, where customers had gathered after seeing promotional offers on products at the showroom.
According to police and customers, the showroom used the abbreviation “CA” in small letters under its offers to indicate that terms and conditions applied. Many customers allegedly failed to notice or understand the abbreviation before visiting the showroom to purchase products at the advertised prices.
When sellers informed the customers about the applicable terms and conditions, some became angry and confronted the shopkeepers, leading to an altercation and commotion at the showroom.
Police later went to the scene after receiving the information and spoke to both sides before bringing the situation under control.
The showroom was subsequently closed over allegations that customers had been misled by the promotional offers and the way the applicable terms and conditions were presented.
Meanwhile, Live Shopping claimed that its showroom was looted during the incident.
The company alleged that several people took various products from the showroom. Multiple posts, photos and videos were shared on its Facebook page, “Live Shopping,” seeking help over the alleged looting.
Dhaka Tribune contacted the number provided on the Live Shopping Facebook page for comment but no one answered.
Pallabi police station Officer-in-Charge Hasan Bashir told Dhaka Tribune that the showroom had been selling products under promotional offers while mentioning that terms and conditions applied.
“The establishment adopted a strategy and wrote ‘CA’ in abbreviated form. This escaped the customers’ notice or they could not understand it. After learning about the offer, customers went to the shop and, after learning about the terms and conditions, expressed their anger at the shopkeepers. A commotion broke out. Later, after receiving the information, we went there, spoke to both sides and brought the situation back to normal,” he said.
The OC said the showroom had been temporarily closed and the customers had left.
He said he was not aware of any looting.
“If any customer has been deceived in the incident, they can take legal action,” he said.

item.title: President calls for refit education system based on culture, national needs
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Friday called for a comprehensive overhaul of the country’s education system, aligning it with Bangladesh’s culture, heritage, employment opportunities and national needs.
“We have to restore our education system afresh by combining our literature, heritage, culture, employment opportunities and all other related necessities,” he said when a delegation of Association of Private Universities of Bangladesh (APUB) met him at Bangabhaban.
“The fragile education system left behind by the previous regime must be revamped afresh. It is necessary to introduce an integrated education system by bringing together various types of education systems,” the President said.
He said indiscriminate approval of low-quality educational institutions during the previous regime had contributed to the creation of an unskilled workforce in the country.
Emphasizing the importance of vocational and technical education, the President said such education could help produce skilled manpower, create employment opportunities abroad and increase the country’s foreign exchange earnings.
During the meeting, the APUB delegation apprised the President of the overall development of higher education, the current state of private universities, efforts to develop skilled human resources and the contribution of private universities to the country’s economic progress.
The delegation sought the President’s cooperation in introducing a performance- and results-based evaluation system and approving new universities based on subject-wise demand, national needs, investment capacity and quality standards.
They called for the introduction of updated curricula, internships, apprenticeships, foreign-language education, artificial intelligence (AI) and professional skills training to ensure that graduates are equipped for employment.
The delegation further urged the President to take steps to transform the University Grants Commission (UGC) into a supportive and development-oriented regulatory body and to formulate an integrated national education system.
Praising the contribution of private universities to the country’s development, the President noted that several private universities of Bangladesh have secured positions in global rankings.
As Chancellor of the universities, the President assured the delegation of all-out cooperation for the development of private universities.

item.description:

The information was provided in a text message sent by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Media and Public Relations Division today, Saturday.

Gulshan police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Daud Hossain told Prothom Alo on Friday afternoon that around 150 to 200 leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations gathered in an alley on Road 3 in Gulshan at around 11:45 am. They tried to bring out a procession.

OC Md Daud Hossain further said that when police moved to disperse them, the participants threw cocktails at the police. Police later fired two rubber bullets to disperse the procession and bring the situation under control.

Police had said that two people were arrested from the scene. They were Abdur Rahim, 49, and Md Arafat, 20. Police also said five cocktails were recovered from their possession.

item.title: Solar power runs school with 2,000 students, AC, computers, over 100 fans
item.description:
It is 8:00 am. The school grounds are filled with the din of the arriving students. Preparations for classes are underway in the classrooms. Fans are running in some rooms, while work is being done on computers in others. An air conditioner (AC) is also running in one of the school’s rooms. Almost all of the school’s electrical equipment runs on solar power.

This was the scene recently at Jorargonj Bouddha High School (JB School) in Mirsarai, Chattogram. Rows of solar panels can be seen on the roofs of two of the school’s three buildings. The 12-kilowatt system is being used to operate more than 100 fans, around 120 lights, several computers and other necessary electrical equipment.

School authorities say that after solar power was installed three years ago, the school’s problems caused by power outages have decreased. In addition, it no longer has to pay electricity bills as high as before. Three years ago, the school used to pay an average of Tk 30,000 a month in electricity bills. Now, it spends Tk 4,000 to Tk 5,000 on electricity.

The school is located beside the Muhuri Project Road near Jorarganj Bazar, about 10 kilometres from Mirsarai upazila headquarters. A recent visit to the school found three concrete buildings surrounding a spacious field. Solar panels have been installed on the roofs of two of them. Classes were being conducted normally in the classrooms from morning to afternoon.

Tushar Kanti Barua is the school’s founder. He is also serving as its head teacher. He said that with the aim of establishing a quality educational institution in Mirsarai, he founded an institution called ‘Shishu Kanan’ in 1988 on a acre of their family land near Jorarganj Bazar. At the request of guardians and to promote education in the area, it was transformed into a full-fledged high school in 1992.

At present, around 2,000 students study the primary and secondary levels at the school. There are 58 teachers and 10 employees. As the number of students has increased, the school’s buildings and classrooms have also expanded. Electricity is now used in around 45 rooms, including classrooms, the teachers’ common room and various administrative rooms. These rooms have electric fans and lights. There is an AC in the head teacher’s room. The accounts room has two computers. All of these run on solar power.

The school’s laboratory has eight computers. When many students use the lab at the same time, it becomes difficult to maintain a normal electricity supply using solar power. The Rural Electricity connection at the school also has to be used. The Rural Electricity connection is also used during natural disasters, when there is no sunlight. Teachers said the connection is needed more during the monsoon and winter.

Head teacher Tushar Kanti Barua said, “We took the initiative to install solar power three years ago with the aim of reducing the pressure of electricity bills. We spent Tk 2.4 million from the school’s fund to install a 12-kilowatt solar power system through a private company in Dhaka.”

Tushar Kanti Barua said, “Now, except on days with severe weather, we get an uninterrupted supply of electricity as needed. Previously, we had to pay an average of Tk 25,000 to Tk 30,000 a month in electricity bills. Now it has fallen below Tk 5,000. Without solar power, we would have to pay Tk 50,000 to Tk 60,000 a month based on current usage.”

Twinkle Barua, an assistant teacher at the school, said, “Since solar power was installed, the uninterrupted electricity supply has made it easier to conduct classes even in hot weather. Students can also study comfortably. This year, the school achieved the best result in the secondary examination in Mirsarai upazila.”

Mirsarai Upazila Executive Officer Somaya Akter praised the school’s initiative. She said solar power systems are cost-effective and provide comfort. The government is also encouraging the use of renewable energy by providing various incentives.

Jorargonj Bouddha High School has set a unique example by bringing the entire school under solar power, and its students are also performing well in board examinations, he added.

item.title: UNICEF internship, students and recent graduates can apply
item.description:
The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has launched its 2026 internship programme for international students and recent graduates.

Internship opportunities are available in various countries and fields. Some positions may offer interns a monthly stipend along with other financial benefits.

UNICEF internships generally last between six and 26 weeks. Students from different countries around the world can apply for these opportunities.

Eligibility

Candidates must meet several requirements to apply for a UNICEF internship. These include:

  • Candidates must be studying at undergraduate, postgraduate or PhD level, or must have completed their degree within the past two years.

  • Candidates must be at least 18 years old.

  • Candidates must have proficiency in at least one of UNICEF’s working languages: English, Spanish or French. Depending on the office where candidates apply, proficiency in the office’s working language may also be required.

Benefits

Benefits may vary depending on the type of internship and the location. These internships may offer a monthly stipend. In some cases, interns may also receive additional financial support towards living expenses, as well as one-off assistance with visa and travel costs.

Nearly half the world’s children exposed to 3 or more climate risks: UNICEF

Required documents

Applicants will generally need documents such as a CV, cover letter, academic transcript and passport. Specific positions may require additional documents.

How to apply

Applicants must apply through the UNICEF careers website.

Application deadline

The application deadline varies from one internship position to another. Therefore, applicants should follow the deadline specified in the vacancy announcement for the position they wish to apply for.

item.title: PM opens Bangladesh Innovation Fair 2026
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today inaugurated a three-day "Bangladesh Innovation Fair 2026".
He laid importance on turning home-grown innovations into commercial products and connecting them directly with the market.
The fair, organized by Ministry of Science and Technology is being held at Novo Theatre at Bijoy Sarani with the theme "Innovate to Market".
The fair aims to build sustainable partnerships among local innovators and innovative organisations, policymakers, entrepreneurs, investors, educational institutions, financial institutions and development partners.
Government and private research organisations, 73 public and private universities, independent researchers, students, emerging startups, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and global investors are participating in the fair.
More than 1,000 new and promising innovations in technology, business, education, health, agriculture, environment and other sectors are being showcased at the event.
The organisers said many promising technologies and ideas are developed at the grassroots level but failed to reach implementation stage due to a lack of policy support, initial funding and institutional cooperation.
Removing such administrative and financial barriers and ensuring intellectual property protection and commercial expansion is the major objective of the fair, they said.
On the second day of the fair tomorrow, a special international session titled ‘Healthcare Innovation for All: Expanding Access to Affordable and Inclusive Healthcare’ will be held.
The session will discuss technologies for delivering affordable, quality healthcare to marginalised people at their doorsteps.
Prime Minister’s wife Dr Zubaida Rahman will attend the tomorrow’s session as the chief guest.
National Board of Revenue (NBR), Department of Patents, Industrial Designs and Trademarks (DPDT) and Foreign Investors’ Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) are strategic partners of the fair, while the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is providing technical support.

item.title: Rizvi stresses education, self-reliance to empower women
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Saturday expressed hope that violence against women including rape, child abuse and all forms of wrongdoing would be eliminated from society.
“We will wipe out rape, violence against women, child abuse and all kinds of wrongdoing from this society,” he said.
He made the remarks before a rally organised in the capital’s Nayapaltan marking the 48th founding anniversary of Jatiyatabadi Mahila Dal.
He said the government led by BNP Chairman and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would ensure women’s civic dignity, right to live and legal rights.
“For this, there are two things. Women must be enlightened through education, and women must become mentally self-reliant. The government has taken many efforts and initiatives to make women mentally self-reliant,” Rizvi said.
He also highlighted education as another key means of empowering women.
Rizvi said the leaders of Jatiyatabadi Mohila Dal are not incompetent and are equally capable of running the state.
“Those who are its leaders, whether at the district level, metropolitan level or central level, none of them is incompetent. They are highly qualified. They are equally capable of running a state and an institution,” he said.
He said BNP’s assumption of power meant that every party worker is now part of the government, not merely those holding official positions.
He said people could now speak and move around freely, while women could travel without fear, and recalled the persecution faced by Mahila Dal leaders during the previous government.
He urged Mahila Dal leaders and activists to closely follow the government’s programmes, particularly its contributions to people and social protection, and communicate those initiatives to the public.
He urged Mahila Dal members to inform people about the government’s measures, particularly those concerning women, saying they are part of both the party and the government.
He said the prime minister’s mother, Begum Khaleda Zia, had made education free up to the intermediate level, with no tuition fees required for girls studying at schools and colleges.
“And her eldest son has said that education up to the degree and honours levels will be free, with no tuition fees for girls’ education,” Rizvi said.
He described the initiatives as public welfare measures aimed at empowering women through education and making them financially self-reliant.
“These programs and initiatives of Tarique Rahman have to be explained to people, communicated to them and spread among them. That is your responsibility because you are part of this party and part of the government,” he said.
Rizvi then inaugurated the colourful rally marking the 48th founding anniversary of Jatiyatabadi Mahila Dal.

item.title: PM urges youth to step forward in nation-building
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has called on the country’s youth to take responsibility for rebuilding the nation, saying no one can stop them if they unite with that goal.
Referring to the events of August 5, 2024, he said the youth had already demonstrated their ability to bring about change by ousting the “fascist regime”.
“We must build this nation. Therefore, the responsibility of rebuilding the state rests with the youth. Everyone must unite to build a clean and tidy country,” he said.
The prime minister made the remarks on Saturday morning while addressing the inauguration of a nationwide three-month dengue prevention and control campaign at the South Plaza of the National Parliament House.
“I seek your assistance. To the best of my knowledge, there are approximately 2.3 million Scouts and 22,000 BNCC members in Bangladesh,” he said.
“Furthermore, excluding primary schools and madrasas, the number of students in high schools, madrasas, colleges and universities across the country is around 15 million. Including primary schools and madrasas, the total reaches 25 million.”
He said the large youth population could play a significant role in transforming the country.
“If such a vast youth population wants to transform the country, it is entirely possible. The youth demonstrated to the entire world on August 5, 2024, that they are capable of bringing about change,” Tarique said.
“The youth initiated that change. So, let us unite here today with the resolve to tackle the dengue problem over the next three months. We may not achieve 100% success, but we can certainly achieve at least 80%.”
The prime minister said the responsibility of rebuilding the country now rests with the youth.
“With so many of us, if we truly wish to rebuild the nation, can anyone stop us? No one can. Now, the responsibility of building the country rests with you,” he said.
He also called for a nationwide cleanliness drive.
“We have gathered here today—thousands of us in this field, and millions more across every district of the country—united by a single goal: to clean our nation and strive to make it free of waste,” he said.
Local Government Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan, State Minister Mir Shahe Alam, Dhaka South City Administrator Abdus Salam and Dhaka North City Administrator Shafiqul Alam Khan Milton also spoke at the event.
After inaugurating the campaign, the prime minister visited various stalls dedicated to dengue awareness.

item.title: Chhatra Dal leader missing after falling into Padma River
item.description:
A local leader of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) went missing after falling into the Padma River when a boat carrying 123 people hit a pillar of the Hardinge Bridge in Bheramara upazila of Kushtia district on Friday night.
The Chhatra Dal leader was identified as Rakibuzzaman Rocky, member secretary of the Shailkupa municipality unit JCD in Jhenaidah.
Mohammad Zahedur Rahman, Officer-in-Charge of Bheramara Police Station, said a group of people hired a boat to visit the Solaiman Shah Shrine in Bheramara from Katla Ghat in Shailkupa of Jhenaidah district.
When the boat was returning after visiting the shrine, it was hit by a strong current, causing it to collide with a pillar of the bridge.
At one point, three people, including Rocky, fell into the river as the rear portion of the bulkhead boat collided with pillar No. 4 of the Hardinge Bridge.
Two of the victims, Liton and Wahab, were rescued, but Rocky remained missing.
Divers from the local fire service conducted a rescue operation but failed to trace Rocky until 1am on Saturday.
Bheramara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mohammad Amirul Arafat, who visited the scene, said darkness and the strong river current were making the rescue operation difficult, while several government units were working at the scene.
Assistant Director of Kushtia Fire Service and Civil Defence Wadud Hossain said: “Due to the strong current in the Padma, it has become difficult to conduct the search operation at night.”

item.title: Is the iPhone 18 Pro a true generational leap?
item.description:
Last Thursday, as I was watching the Apple September event, the exact moment Tim Cook stepped aside and moved John Ternus toward center stage —"no no no, not me, that's your guy, that's your opener”—felt less like a casual baton pass and more like a gravitational pivot the industry had been waiting for.
The engineer who built Apple's silicon transition from the inside became its CEO at the exact moment Apple shipped its most coherent product generation in a decade: the M6 Mac Mini, the M5 MacBooks, M5 Max, M5 Ultra, and the A20 Pro iPhone.
Same commitment, across every device Apple makes, simultaneously. This is more than a product refresh cycle.
Apple does not believe the future of AI lives in a data centre.
It believes the future of AI lives in your hand, on your lap or your desk — running locally, privately, without a server, without your data leaving your device.
Apple spent the past four years building the best inference machine that you and I, the general population, can actually buy.
Ternus made that philosophy explicit from his very first keynote: the iPhone is no longer just a smartphone; it is an intelligent personal hub you start your day with.
The iPhone 18 Pro is the first product built explicitly around that philosophy. Everything Apple did inside this device is the engineering consequence of that single bet.
Welcome to Ramgageddon
At a glance, the 18 Pro and Pro Max look very similar to last year’s 17 Pros.
You still get the aluminium unibody with Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back, but they are now all color-matched instead of two-tone.
This year you can enjoy the new flagship Burgundy color, alongside Glacier, Silver, and finally, matte Black.
However, the first major upgrade for the Pros is the price. Given the hyper memory inflation we have seen across the entire Apple product line—driven by the massive RAM inflation for AI—both models are now up by $100.
The 18 Pro starts at $1,199 and the Pro Max at $1,299, with a new 2TB storage option.
That stings less than what Apple quietly did to the models it did not update. The iPhone Air moves to $1,099, base 17 to $899, and the 17e to $699. There was no iPhone 18.
Today, we are here for the Pros.
A20 Pro: The desktop class architecture
After three years of 3nm chips, the A20 Pro is Apple's first smartphone chip built on cutting-edge 2-nanometer technology.
The CPU holds the same 6-core arrangement as the A19 Pro: two super cores running 20% faster than their predecessors, and four efficiency cores, all integrated with neural accelerators for low-latency, on-device AI.
But the GPU moves to a 7-core design, accommodating up to 40% performance increase driven by expanded internal bandwidth and a new generation of neural accelerators with 2x faster 8-bit floating-point math.
But neither the CPU nor the GPU is where the real change happened.
The Neural Engine is. Apple doubled it. The A20 Pro features a dual 16-core Neural Engine just like the newly introduced M6 Mac Mini, delivering twice the AI compute of the A19 Pro.
For context, the 32 Neural Engine cores were previously reserved for the Mac Ultra.
Apple has pulled that architecture into a phone.
Feeding all of it results in a 50% increase in memory bandwidth— the widest memory interface Apple has ever shipped in an iPhone.
Raw core counts are just ideas without the bandwidth to keep them going when you need them.
Packing this much compute into a smartphone chassis created a thermal constraint that a conventional vapor chamber could not resolve.
Apple resolved it at the silicon packaging level.
The A20 Pro introduces custom chip packaging directly inspired by the M-series packaging, with the silicon die now sitting side-by-side with memory rather than stacked beneath it.
This single repositioning removes the memory from the thermal path of the SoC.
The chip sits flush against the vapor chamber. What previously acted as insulation is now out of the way entirely.
The vapor chamber itself was rebuilt from scratch. It carries three times the surface area compared to the 17 Pro's, cycling deionized water continuously across a structure made from 80% recycled stainless steel.
A larger graphite plate handles the remaining thermal load. The critical addition is nanotwin copper, an industry-first material that moves heat specifically away from the display while maintaining structural strength.
The combined result is a 40% improvement in not just peak benchmark numbers, but sustained performance over the 17 Pro, and a 2x improvement over the 16 Pro.
The logic board was also redesigned entirely to fit a larger battery.
The result is visible in the most honest metric available: weight.
The iPhone 18 Pros are the heaviest Pro Apple has ever shipped.
Variable aperture: Hardware, finally
The camera is arguably the most important part of the iPhone experience, and with the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple introduced its biggest upgrade in years: a true Variable Aperture.
Aperture controls how much light enters the sensor and dictates depth of field.
On every previous iPhone, you had only two ways of controlling the light: ISO and shutter speed.
A fixed aperture, like the f/1.78, was the constraint you worked around. Cranking ISO to handle low light caused graininess because you were amplifying sensor sensitivity without controlling the incoming light itself. The physics were always working against you.
The new 48MP Fusion main camera removes that constraint.
Apple has created a system of six laser-cut polymer blades, each thinner than a human hair, all controlled by a custom rotor mechanism. This rotor can mechanically adjust the aperture between four specific positions: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0.
If you open it up to f/1.48 or f/1.8, you are letting in 50% more light, which is perfect for low-light and astrophotography.
But if you stop it down to f/4.0, you can really make sure the entire scene is in focus.
For the average person, this means no more blurry faces in the back row of group dinner shots, and no more grainy, unusable night photos.
This is the first time you actually have control over depth of field at a hardware level.
The frictionless ecosystem
The N1 networking chip is a transition management story. Real-world throughput lives in the seams—the exact moment your phone shifts from Wi-Fi 7 to cellular or routes a call across two simultaneous connections without dropping a word.
The N1 is engineered specifically to make those handoffs completely invisible.
Pair that with Apple’s in-house C2 modem packaged alongside the A20 Pro—guaranteeing a noticeable bump to internet speeds and reliability even when you are stuck in traditional dead zones, and the hardware finally catches up to how we actually live and work on the move.
Additionally, iPhone Handoff routes a single phone number transparently across two iPhones to whichever iPhone you pick up via invisible, modem-level carrier negotiation.
If you carry a work phone and a personal phone, this feature alone will fundamentally change how you navigate your day.
Apple also managed to fit part of Face ID under the display, allowing the Dynamic Island to shrink 35% compared to the 17 Pro. It is now far more useful, capable of displaying three live activities at a glance. A small change that compounds in usefulness when the device is routing this much information at once.
Another key improvement is the battery life. The iPhone 18 Pro carries a 4,056 mAh cell, delivering 36 hours of video playback compared to 33 hours on the 17 Pro.
The Pro Max is the more dramatic story — 5,391 mAh, 45 hours of video playback.
That is at least 6 hours more than the 17 Pro Max, driven by a significantly larger battery cell alongside the chip’s efficiency improvements.
On eSIM-only models, the numbers are even bigger: 4,288 and 5,567 mAh. If endurance is your primary concern, the Max has never made a stronger case for itself.
The charging architecture now matches the power draw: 50% charge in 15 minutes, roughly 20% faster than the previous generation.
Just five minutes of wired charging delivers approximately 6 hours of video playback.
For a device running sustained workloads across a full day, that is more than a convenience feature.
The intelligence layer
The 32-core Neural Engine is not a Siri feature. Siri is a Neural Engine feature. The chip came first.
Every improvement in Siri AI — on-device personal context across apps, real-time action inside 300,000 third-party applications, expressive voices — exists only because Apple built the hardware to run it locally, without a server, without latency, without your data leaving the device. That is the architecture. Siri is what sits on top of it.
One precision matters here. Apple's on-device models are excellent at what they do. Frontier AI capabilities — GPT-4 class reasoning, complex multi-step analysis — still run in data centres regardless of what device you hold.
The 32-core Neural Engine does not change that ceiling.
What it changes is the floor: the baseline of what this device can do privately, instantly, and without a network connection. That is the bet Apple is making.
Together with state-of-the-art hardware, a handful of incredibly handy software-level improvements have arrived.
Pro controls make the manual capabilities accessible without requiring a third-party app: aperture selection between four positions, shutter speed, white balance, and a histogram for exposure monitoring, all built into the native camera interface.
Photographic Styles received an upgrade. Apple added texture and grain control, allowing you to fine-tune the interplay between light and shadow or adjust skin texture to elevate the emotion of a scene.
You can balance color and texture simultaneously, and crucially, reverse or change these edits at any time.
The 18 Pro brings a much-needed double-tap tracking feature that keeps your focus on any subject, no matter where they move around in the frame.
Plus, it comes with stunning 4K Dolby Vision HDR time-lapses and Cinematic mode effects that you can add to your regular videos after you have captured them—now with 60 frames per second for smooth half-speed playback.
This transforms the device into an uncompromising mobile camera rig.
AudioMix receives a meaningful update too: music now joins voice as a supported input type.
For field production, this eliminates the binary choice between capturing your subject’s voice or the acoustic environment surrounding them.
Combined with ProRes Log recording and Smart Focus Tracking, the 18 Pro now becomes a true camera-to-edit solution for run-and-gun production.
This is exactly why Samsung has not quite won over the “Shot on iPhone” crowd.
Finally, “Image Authenticity” is where Apple makes its most consequential long-term statement.
Apple goes beyond fallible watermarks. Supporting the SynthID standard to identify AI-generated images is the industry baseline, but Apple is going a step further with the “Apple Reference Image.”
Now you can mathematically prove the authenticity of a photo taken on an iPhone 18 Pro.
Apple Reference Image starts in the most secure way possible: with the sensor.
The new main sensor securely and digitally signs photo metadata at the pixel level the exact moment of capture.
Private Cloud Compute develops that signed data into an unalterable image in the Photos a pp that acts as a digital negative to visually confirm what was actually in the shot.
This reference photo lives alongside the regular editable photo for flexibility, setting a standard that should become a universal standard for every camera on Earth.
Verdict
What does it signal about the industry?
The spec war — thinner, lighter, brighter, marginally better camera benchmarks — is structurally over. Apple has now replaced it with a different competition entirely: sustained compute density.
For the past two years, the tech industry settled into a comfortable consensus: Apple was losing the AI race.
OpenAI rewrote what an assistant could do. Google embedded Gemini across its entire product suite. Meta open-sourced its models and dared everyone to keep up.
Apple, meanwhile, partnered with OpenAI and now Google. The industry read that as surrender.
They are wrong.
The writer is a contributor and tech enthusiast

item.title: Zero IRF: Who will bear the costs of free service?
item.description:
Fire, water, open space, and air are mankind's original commons.
While air remains the most free-flowing of them all, it still requires money under certain conditions, and the breath in our lungs carries a cost in today's post-industrial era.
Let us draw a parallel to the Bangladesh Bank's recent decision to slash down to zero the interchange reimbursement fee or IRF, which is the vital earning source of the participating institutions that provide mobile financial services (MFS).
Not just this monetary transaction facility, but also any utilities free of costs -- be it telecommunications and banking services or use of electricity -- could have been considered the most loved thing to modern people, had there been no charges!
The central bank has made the policy shift by cutting IRF to be zero and MDR can be set at zero with the lifting of 1% floor price effective from October 1, 2026.
This directive for 'Bangla QR' system has been issued to further popularize digital payments.
It allows customers to make direct payments simply by scanning a merchant's QR (Quick Response) code using their bank or MFS apps, a revolutionary step towards attaining transparency in daily commerce and a cashless society.
In Bangladesh, we expect that the government provides energy subsidy without actually targeting the vulnerable groups who need and deserve it.
As a result, such policy turns unsustainable, and the people have to pay multiple prices to get access to energy. Also, the farmers have been incurring losses over the years as a consequence of a populist policy of, say, for example, keeping rice price low.
Now, the question arises: would a zero IRF and MDR not expose the entire digital payment ecosystem to severe structural risks as the measure removes an 'organic revenue model that funds network infrastructure, security upgrades and fraud prevention'?
None can deny that zero fees are consumer-friendly, only on paper, however. Industry innovators apprehend that this decision would jeopardize the institutions that have invested in building the digital payment infrastructure.
Many others may either ignore or be unaware of the fact that behind every seamless QR transaction lies a complex web of expenses: technology maintenance, agent incentives, distribution networks, mobile network operator charges, customer service, and settlement costs.
This means removing the IRF and MDR strips the platforms of their capacity to recover these essential operating costs.
Similar digital payment was 'free' in India where the government has borne the costs by giving subsidies, but that subsidy, too, is going to be withdrawn anytime.
Given the current fiscal constraints, it is not advisable either that the government of Bangladesh subsidize the costs of going cashless.
At the same time, making zero IRF and MDR to pave the way for popularizing Bangla QR is tantamount to punishing MFS operators who have made investments and driven the vast majority of digital financial transactions.
The process of converting hard cash into digital balance (cash-in) and vice versa (cash-out) relies on a massive network of human agents and distributors, according to the business model.
Managing this expansive infrastructure is financed through a delicate balance of transaction fees, service commissions, and merchant discount rates or MDR.
The government would lose revenues in the form of value-added tax (VAT) for every transaction under this model.
The MFS provider's subsidy for a single Tk1,000 cash-in transaction could stand at Tk6.40.
This begs another question: If the financial spine of the existing digital infrastructure is weakened in the name of incentivizing cashless transactions, who will foot the bill in the long run?
Cuts in fees for agents under the circumstances may work as a disincentive for this army of people, numbering around 2.4 million to remain engaged in MFS.
This human network has democratized financial services, reaching the under-banked and unbanked masses even in remote places.
If the agent-driven ecosystem is dismantled to force a new digital payment model prematurely, years of hard-earned progress in financial inclusion may be reversed.
In zero IRF and MDR regime, some desperate merchants and/or agents may find incentive to make fake payments and still take certain commissions bypassing the system. Transactions of ill-gotten money or money laundering through fake payments cannot be ruled out.
Already allegations have it that some agents and merchants are exploiting Bangla QR codes to facilitate informal cash-out services for customers without any actual exchange of goods or services.
On paper, these look like progressive digital payments, but in reality, they are merely disguised cash withdrawals.
Such practice would artificially inflate official digital transaction data; it distorts the true picture of digital commerce in the country. Industry experts warn that a zero-IRF and MDR policy will likely amplify this malpractice.
An unintended consequence of this policy is likely to be the squeezing of MFS providers, who may eventually be forced to impose new charges on basic cash-in services.
This would create a lose-lose scenario: the government's revenues contract, while the transaction costs for ordinary citizens rise.
Since Bangla QR is deeply intertwined with the broader digital payment grid, a one-sided measure of introducing zero fees may be counterproductive.
Thus, the central bank may think of devising a balanced tariff structure through discussions with the stakeholders.
If QR codes become a tool to bypass standard cash-out channels without driving real retail commerce, it is feared that Bangla QR will end up deviating from its core objective of fostering a genuine cashless economy.
Salahuddin Bablu is a journalist

item.title: FIFA rebuffs Morocco claim over 2030 World Cup final
item.description:
FIFA said on Friday that a decision on the venue for the 2030 World Cup final would be made "in due course", after Moroccan football federation president Fouzi Lekjaa said the showpiece match would be staged in Morocco.
Morocco, Spain and Portugal are co-hosting the 2030 tournament and have already begun competing for the right to stage the final, with Madrid's Santiago Bernabeu and a planned 115,000-seat stadium in Benslimane, near Casablanca, viewed as the leading contenders.
Lekjaa said on Wednesday that the final would take place in Morocco.
"Benslimane province will host the World Cup final. Whether some people like it or not," Lekjaa said during a public meeting in the region, according to video published by local media.
However, FIFA said no decision had yet been taken.
"As communicated on 5 August 2026, a decision will be made by FIFA in due course," a FIFA spokesperson told AFP on Friday.
The comments prompted reaction in Spain, where Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho backed the Santiago Bernabeu as the ideal venue for the final.
"I would like the final to be in Lisbon, but I'm already happy that a country like ours will have at least one match (at the World Cup)," the Portuguese coach told reporters on Friday.
"If you can play in a legendary, historic stadium, where some of the greatest players in history have played, the stadium of the most important club in the history of football, then I think it should be here," Mourinho said, referring to the Bernabeu.
"If I were Benfica's coach, I would tell you exactly the same thing."

item.title: Razaullah’s fearless Edgbaston assault gives Pakistan a lift
item.description:
Pakistan pacer Razaullah produced a stunning counterattacking display on Test debut to give Pakistan a much-needed boost in their World Test Championship clash against England at Edgbaston.
The 21-year-old walked in at 9 with the score at 312/7 and Pakistan still needing another 8 runs to make England bat again, and went on an assault, smashing 81 from just 63 deliveries.
His nine sixes equalled the record for most sixes by a debutant in a Test innings and helped Pakistan set England a fourth-innings target of 130 after being pushed to the brink.
Razaullah’s approach was one of fearless aggression, particularly against the short ball, as he took on Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Josh Tongue.
“I was being selective with which balls to slog, but they all seemed within range,” he said after the conclusion of Day 3.
“I wanted to take it as deep as possible. I wasn’t scared of pace.
“I wanted to punish the balls from Archer that landed on a hard length.
“There’s nothing to be scared of when you’re playing for your country.
“I was just enjoying myself.”
At Edgbaston, he backed himself against an England attack that had repeatedly troubled Pakistan’s batters during the series, which gave the home side an unassailable 2-0 lead from the opening two Tests.
“My favourite ball [to face] is the short ball. I just believed in myself.
“I thought if I played 50 balls, I’d get a positive result. And thankfully that happened.”
Razaullah’s intent was matched by the enjoyment he displayed at the crease, soaking in the reception as the Edgbaston crowd stood up to commemorate his fighting spirit.
“I enjoyed the standing ovation.
“I like to enjoy life and I was relishing the moment.”
England will begin Day 4 with the bat, needing 130 runs to make it 3-0 in the three-match series.

item.title: Zverev holds off Khachanov, Shelton powers past Tiafoe to reach US Open final
item.description:
Top seed Alexander Zverev out-gunned Karen Khachanov to reach his third straight Grand Slam final on Friday, rolling into the US Open title match with a straight sets win.
Big-serving Ben Shelton overpowered American compatriot Frances Tiafoe in four sets to reach the first Grand Slam final of his career.
Zverev, who followed up his maiden major at the French Open with a runner-up finish at Wimbledon, saved two set points in the final tiebreaker to close out the 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) victory.
He'll face Ben Shelton in Sunday's championship match.
The German predicted an "absolutely epic" contest between the two Americans, after which he'll be out to thwart the winner's bid to become the first American man in 23 years to lift a Grand Slam trophy.
"Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday," said Zverev, who came agonizingly close to the US Open title in 2020 before falling to Dominic Thiem in five sets.
After a somewhat inauspicious start to the tournament, spending nine hours and 26 minutes on court in laborious five-set victories in the first and second rounds, Zverev has steadily upped his game.
He needed two hours and 57 minutes to deny 50th-ranked Khachanov's bid to become the lowest-ranked Grand Slam finalist since number 54 Marcos Baghdatis at the 2006 Australian Open.
But the Russian, who fell to Zverev in the Olympic gold medal match in Tokyo in 2021, put up a spirited challenge in the second and third sets.
Unable to make any real headway in the first set, Khachanov fell a quick break down in the second.
The Russian couldn't resist a grin when he snuck a passing shot by Zverev to open the fourth game, and flung his arm into the air in celebration three points later when a forehand winner gave him his first break chance of the match.
Zverev double faulted to hand him a break that leveled the set at 2-2.
Khachanov had another chance two games later when Zverev's backhand into the net to end a 32-shot rally gave him a break point.
But the German came up with a big serve and escaped the danger as they went to the tiebreaker, where Khachanov denied Zverev on two set points with thumping forehand and a brilliant backhand down the line before Zverev closed out the set.
Neither player mustered a break point in a tense third set. Khachanov had a chance to extend the match when he took a 6-4 lead in the tiebreaker, but after a pair of forehand errors from the Russian Zverev came up with his 15th ace and sealed the win on the next point when Khachanov sent a forehand long.
Eighth-seeded Shelton blasted 20 aces on his way to a thrilling 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory on the Arthur Ashe Stadium court that sends the 23-year-old into Sunday's championship match against top-seeded Alexander Zverev of Germany.
A pulsating all-American semi-final had seen both players vying to reach a Grand Slam final for the first time.
Shelton -- who took down defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in the quarter-finals -- will now have the chance to become the first American man to win a Grand Slam title since 2003, when Andy Roddick triumphed at the US Open.
"It's a lot of emotion," Shelton said in an on-court interview after a win that was watched by a star-studded New York crowd.
"My dad, my mom have sacrificed a lot for me to be in this position today. My dad lost his mom earlier this year, and she's the reason that he was able to play tennis.
"Without her, there's no Ben Shelton standing here today. So this one is for her. And I'm gonna need you guys on Sunday to to bring the energy. I'm going for it. I'm gonna leave it all on the court.
Earlier, Tiafoe got off to a bright start, claiming the first set after breaking when Shelton uncharacteristically double-faulted to trail at 5-4.
Tiafoe held to love to clinch the first set but Shelton came flying out of the blocks to start the second.
An early break helped him into a 2-0 lead before Tiafoe responded with a break to level at 2-2.
Yet with Tiafoe's serve increasingly erratic, Shelton grabbed another break in the eighth game to go 5-3 up and then held to level.
The momentum was all with Shelton and Tiafoe had to fight off two break points before holding early in the third set.
However Shelton – who had one serve initially clocked at 158mph before it was later adjusted to 144mph -- made no mistake in the fifth game with a break to go 3-2 up.
Tiafoe needed to hold to keep the set alive in the ninth game, and a furious arm-wrestle saw the 11th seed once again save three break and set points.
Shelton though earned his fourth break point after pouncing on Tiafoe's second serve once more, scorching a backhand return down the line.
Shelton converted that when Tiafoe netted a forehand to find himself 2-1 down.
The fourth set went with serve until the 12th game, when Shelton grabbed the crucial break to seal victory.
